# ultrafast: full site text

> ultrafast is an open-source GPU video engine for agents. Shaders, 3D, motion type and camera optics, written by your agent and rendered on the GPU at hundreds of frames a second, with no browser in the loop. Your agent checks and reviews every frame before it exports.

# ultrafast · Shot on the GPU · Open-source video engine for agents

> Shot on the GPU. Shaders, 3D, motion type and camera optics, written by your agent and rendered on the GPU. An open-source video engine for coding agents.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/

Open source · Apache-2.0 or MIT

# ultrafast: video shot on the GPU

Shaders, 3D, motion type and real camera optics, written by your agent and rendered at GPU speed.

`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` [Read the quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)

macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux. [Other ways to install](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/#install>)

Or tell your agent `“Go to ultrafast.mov and make…”`

clay.json · excerpt

```
{
  "format": { "width": 1080,
    "height": 1920, "fps": 30 },
  "nodes": {
    "vessel": {
      "op": "shader",
      "params": {
        "code": "// a lathe, its profile keyed…",
        "u4": { "keys": [ … ] } } },
    "title": {
      "op": "text",
      "params": {
        "text": "Spin something new.",
        "font": "ultrafast:display",
        "size": 176 } },
    …
  },
  "output": "grain"
}
``` 

[Video: Spin something new: a 10-second pottery class teaser](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/clay.mp4) 

**1.68 s** to export these 10 seconds at 1080×1920.

Rust · Vulkan on Linux and WSL2 · Metal on macOS · 70 ops · 20 MCP tools · a live player

How it works

## A frame is a stack of plates.

Each plate is a node in one JSON document. Point at a line to find its plate; click to pull it.

clay.json · 1080×1920 · 30 fps · 10 s

3D and 2D

## 3D, 2D, or both.

One engine renders 3D models, type, vector shapes, charts and footage, and composites them in the same frame. No Blender, no After Effects, no plugins: all of it is in the document.

[All the films](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/>)

  * ![The HOLM 35 lens from the launch film, rendered in 3D by ultrafast](https://ultrafast.mov/img/lens_front.webp)3D
  * ![The same lens rendered again with the camera turned 84 degrees](https://ultrafast.mov/img/lens_side.webp)3D, camera turned 84°
  * ![The concert poster: Swiss-style type and vector shapes](https://ultrafast.mov/img/mix_poster.webp)2D: type and shapes
  * ![The pottery class teaser: a 3D pot on its wheel under the title and details](https://ultrafast.mov/img/mix_clay.webp)both: a 3D pot under set type

The lens and the pot are geometry and materials in their documents, lit and rendered by ultrafast, not made in a 3D app. Turning the camera is one more render of the same node: about 0.3 s.

Speed

## 894 frames a second

1920×1080 · 6-sample motion blur · one RTX 5090

press log

    894 fps
launch film, 16 s
    4.88 s
simulation, 15 s
    1.06 s
class teaser, 10 s
    1.68 s

no browser in the loop

[Video: HOLM 35 f/1.4, a launch film for a camera lens](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/product.mp4) 

**4.88 s** to export this 16-second launch film: 480 frames at 1920×1080.

Review

## First draft: eight findings. Second: none.

`uf review` read all 300 frames in 4.7 s.

![Contact sheet of the first draft from uf sheet, frames at 0.55, 2.6, 4.5 and 7.5 seconds. Frame one is a white flash, the title runs off the right edge, the studio name is too dark to read and the details are tiny.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/proof_draft.webp)

  1. **flashing** more than 3 flashes per second: a photosensitive seizure risk (WCAG 2.3.1)
  2. **clipped** "Pottery class" runs off the frame (right by 40 px)
  3. **low contrast ×2** "HALDEN CLAY STUDIO" never reaches readable contrast (best 1.6:1, want 3:1 or more); "118 TANNER STREET" 1.6:1
  4. **too brief** "First class free" is readable for 0.4 s; 3 words need about 0.9 s
  5. **small text ×3** set at 20 px; below about 24 px it is hard to read on a phone

![Contact sheet of the second draft at the same moments: no flash, the title fits, the studio name and the details read.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/proof_approved.webp) 0 findings

  1. `new`: starts from a template
  2. `check`: finds problems without rendering
  3. `review`: reads every frame
  4. `export`: the teaser in 1.68 s

Edits

## Edit it by asking.

Your agent edits the document, not the pixels. One sentence changed one node: the pot's shape, its camera and its shader. The type, light and timing stayed as they were.

This works today in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI with `uf mcp`.

Coming soon The ChatGPT app and the Claude connector, for making videos in a chat. [Join the waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/#apps>)

A 10-second vertical teaser for my pottery class. Saturdays, first class free.

[Video: The teaser, first version: a vase thrown on the wheel](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/clay.mp4)

agentclay.json · 10 s · 1080×1920 · `review` 0 findings

Make it a wide bowl instead of a vase.

[Video: The teaser after the edit: a wide bowl](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/clay-bowl.mp4)

agentedited 1 node, `vessel`. The type, light and timing are untouched.

Compare

## No browser in the loop.

Remotion and HyperFrames draw each frame in headless Chrome and capture it. ultrafast draws it on the GPU, and your agent writes a quarter to a third fewer tokens than for Remotion.

[Full comparison](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/>)

| ultrafast| Remotion| HyperFrames  
---|---|---|---  
Draws each frame with| GPU kernels, Metal or Vulkan| headless Chrome, a screenshot per frame| headless Chrome, captured frame by frame  
You write| one JSON document| a React project| HTML, CSS and JavaScript  
Output tokens for a 10 s short| about 1,234| about 1,868| about 1,680  
Export, same machine ([benchmark](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>))| 0.78 s for 10 s of captioned NASA footage, 1080×1920, end to end| 6.69 s at its fastest setting found; 8.53 s with its default command| 4.46 s at its fastest setting found; 5.05 s with its default command  
Agents review their frames| `check`, `review`, `inspect`, frames and contact sheets| no built-in review| no built-in review  
Licence| Apache-2.0 or MIT| free up to 3 people; companies pay per render or per seat| Apache-2.0  
Hosted rendering| ultrafast Cloud, coming soon ([waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>)); `uf serve` on your GPU today| none: Lambda in your AWS account| HeyGen credits, or your own Lambda or Cloud Run  
  
Export times are from the [benchmark](<https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/>); other Remotion and HyperFrames figures are from their own docs, November 2026. [Sources](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/#sources>).

Questions

## Common questions.

What is ultrafast?

An open-source video engine built for AI agents. A video is a JSON document of nodes (footage, type, shapes, 3D, effects); ultrafast checks it, shows the agent its frames and renders it on the GPU at hundreds of frames a second.

Do I need a GPU?

Yes, for now: a Mac with Apple silicon, or a computer with a Vulkan GPU on Linux or Windows (through WSL2). ultrafast Cloud, which renders on hosted GPUs, is coming soon: [join the waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).

Can it edit my own footage?

Yes. Cut, trim, speed-ramp, reframe, grade, key and caption video files, mix in music and voiceover, and add titles, logos and charts. The [footage examples](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/#footage>) cut, caption and grade NASA film and sound.

Is the 3D in the examples rendered by ultrafast?

Yes. The pot, the lens, the compass, the chrome ring, the Earth and the Moon are geometry and materials written in each film's document. ultrafast lights and renders them on the GPU every frame, in the same pass as the type. Nothing was filmed, and nothing was made in a 3D app.

Which sizes and formats can it make?

Any size and frame rate: 9:16, 1:1, 4:5, 16:9, 21:9 or your own, up to 4K. Exports are MP4 or MOV in H.264 or HEVC, with sound.

How is it different from Remotion or HyperFrames?

They draw each frame in headless Chrome and screenshot it. ultrafast draws on the GPU with no browser. On one RTX 5090 workstation, three 10-second videos exported in 0.66 to 0.78 s; at their fastest settings, Remotion took 3.1 to 8.6 times as long and HyperFrames 4.6 to 5.7 times ([benchmark](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>)). It also gives agents tools to check and review their videos. See the [comparison](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/>).

Does an agent use fewer tokens with ultrafast?

Yes: a quarter to a third fewer than with Remotion, and a fifth to a quarter fewer than with HyperFrames. Measured on the same 10-second short (tiktoken o200k_base): 1,234 tokens across the files the agent writes in ultrafast, 1,868 for Remotion and 1,680 for HyperFrames; counting only what is typed after each tool's scaffold, 1,218, 1,660 and 1,500. See [tokens](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/#tokens>).

What does it cost?

Nothing. The engine is free under Apache-2.0 or MIT, for commercial use, at any scale.

Is there a hosted version?

Not yet. ultrafast Cloud will run the same engine on hosted GPUs with one API key, and the ChatGPT app and the Claude connector will run on it. [Join the waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>) for one email when it opens.

## curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh

`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` [Read the quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)

Want it hosted? [Join the ultrafast Cloud waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).

# Quickstart

## Install

One binary, `ultrafast`, with `uf` as its short name. On macOS (Apple silicon) or Linux x86_64:

```
curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh
``` 

[The script](<https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh>) downloads the prebuilt release for your machine from [GitHub releases](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/releases>), checks its SHA-256, unpacks it into `~/.ultrafast` and links `ultrafast` and `uf` into `~/.local/bin`. Or pick one of these:

```
brew install ultrafastmov/tap/ultrafast    # macOS and Linux, prebuilt
cargo install ultrafast                    # from crates.io, Rust 1.91 or later
docker run --gpus all ghcr.io/ultrafastmov/ultrafast:latest info
``` 

Or tell your agent “Go to ultrafast.mov and make…” and finish the sentence: it reads [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>), installs ultrafast and makes the video. Say “go to”: a bare “ultrafast.mov” reads to an agent like a video file.

It renders with **Metal** on macOS and **Vulkan** on Linux, and on Windows through WSL2 ([WINDOWS.md](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/blob/main/docs/WINDOWS.md>)). Exports on Vulkan use ffmpeg, and on Linux voiceover and OCR use eSpeak NG and Tesseract. The Docker image includes all of them; the prebuilt binaries include everything else. No GPU? [ultrafast Cloud](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>) is coming soon.

```
$ uf info
backend: vulkan
device:  NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
``` 

## Your first video

Start from a template, look at it, then export it.

```
uf new vertical film.json                       # 1080×1920, 6 s, already looks finished
uf check film.json                              # problems, before anything renders
uf sheet film.json --count 9 --out sheet.png    # nine frames in one image
uf live film.json                               # plays it; edits show on the next frame
uf review film.json --safe social               # what a viewer would trip over
uf export film.json film.mp4                    # hardware-encoded mp4
``` 

Other templates: `title`, `square`, `promo`, `explainer` and `product`. Edit the words in `film.json` and run `uf export` again.

## What you just made

A video is one JSON document: a `format`, a graph of `nodes`, and the node to `output`. Nodes are sources (footage, type, shapes, 3D), effects and composites; any param can be animated.

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "format": { "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "fps": 60, "duration": 4.0 },
  "output": "comp",
  "nodes": {
    "bg":   { "op": "gradient", "params": { "a": "#0b0b1a", "b": "#2a1650" } },
    "disc": { "op": "shape", "params": {
      "kind": "circle", "color": "#ff7a2e", "size": [360, 360],
      "center": { "keys": [
        { "t": 0, "v": [560, 540], "ease": "in_out_cubic" },
        { "t": 4, "v": [1360, 540] }
      ] } } },
    "comp": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "disc", "bg": "bg" } }
  }
}
``` 

The whole vocabulary is in [the op reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/>), and `uf ops` prints it as JSON. The shape of a document is in [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>).

## The loop

This is how an agent works, and how you should too:

  1. **Start** from `uf new` or a copy of an example.
  2. **Check** : `uf check` reports unknown ops, misspelled params (with suggestions), wrongly shaped values, broken shaders and missing files, without rendering.
  3. **Look** : `uf sheet` for motion at a glance, `uf render --at 2.5` for one exact frame, `uf inspect --at 2.5` for which node drew what.
  4. **Review** : `uf review` renders the film and reports unreadable, clipped, overlapping, tiny or too-brief text, text under social app buttons, and flashing faster than three times a second.
  5. **Export** : `uf export`, hardware-encoded with sound and motion blur.

## Connect an agent

`uf mcp` serves all of this as 20 MCP tools over stdio. Frames and contact sheets come back as images, so the agent sees what it made.

```
claude mcp add ultrafast -- uf mcp
``` 

Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and remote MCP over HTTP are on the [MCP page](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>). Agents can also read [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>) and every page of these docs as Markdown.

## Run it as a service

`uf serve` puts the engine behind an HTTP API and remote MCP on your GPU, with one API key, for apps, the [SDKs](<https://ultrafast.mov/integrations/#sdks>) and agents on other machines.

```
uf serve --port 8080                   # prints its API key at first start
export ULTRAFAST_API_KEY=uf_live_...
jq '{document: ., output: {inline: true}}' film.json |
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/render -H "Authorization: Bearer $ULTRAFAST_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @- -o film.mp4
``` 

The requests are in [HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>). A hosted version, ultrafast Cloud, is coming soon: [join the waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).

# The document format · ultrafast docs

> An ultrafast video is one JSON document: a format, a graph of nodes, animated params and timing windows. The full shape, with examples.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/

Docs

# The document

A video is one JSON file. Here is its whole shape.

## Start

  * [Quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)
  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

## Guides

## For agents

  * [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>)
  * [This page as Markdown](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/index.md>)

**On this page**

  1. Shape
  2. format
  3. nodes
  4. Params and animation
  5. timing
  6. components
  7. Assets, colour, type
  8. Schema and versions

## Shape

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "format": { "width": 1080, "height": 1920, "fps": 30, "duration": 10,
              "motion_blur": { "samples": 6, "shutter": 0.5 } },
  "nodes": {
    "<id>": { "op": "<op>", "params": { }, "inputs": { }, "timing": { } }
  },
  "components": { },
  "output": "<id of the node to render>"
}
``` 

Documents are plain files you can diff, template and edit. The engine reloads a document when it changes, so an agent can write it directly or through `uf edit`.

## format

  * `width`, `height`: any size, in pixels. Change them and frame-relative layout (blocks, captions, `fit`, stacks) follows.
  * `fps`, `duration`: frames per second and seconds.
  * `motion_blur`: `samples` and `shutter`, plus `max_samples` for whips and fast pans. Each moving layer is blurred on its own, as a compositor does; footage and shaders hold at the frame's time.

## nodes

Each node has an `op`, its `params`, its `inputs` (other nodes, by id, on named ports) and optional `timing`. Sources have no inputs; effects take a `source`; composites take `fg` and `bg`.

```
"clip":  { "op": "video", "params": { "src": "launch.mp4", "fit": "cover", "start": 12 } },
"grade": { "op": "grade", "inputs": { "source": "clip" }, "params": { "look": 2, "amount": 0.6 } },
"title": { "op": "block", "params": { "kind": "title", "title": "Artemis I", "kicker": "16 Nov 2022" } },
"comp":  { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "title", "bg": "grade" } }
``` 

Generators (`solid`, `gradient`, `noise`, shaders) are infinite: crop or transform them into panels. Paths and text stay vector until they are rasterized, so a `transform` directly on them stays sharp at any scale. The planner fuses chains of nodes into one GPU kernel and skips what can't be seen.

## Params and animation

Any param can be a constant or animated:

```
"size": 64
"position": { "keys": [ { "t": 0, "v": [540, 2100], "ease": "out_expo" },
                        { "t": 0.8, "v": [540, 960] } ] }
"rotation": { "keys": [ { "t": 0, "v": 0 }, { "t": 1, "v": 10 } ], "repeat": "pingpong" }
"position": { "wiggle": { "frequency": 2, "amplitude": 10, "base": [540, 960] } }
"opacity":  { "expr": "0.5 + 0.5 * sin(t * 3)" }
``` 

  * **Keys** : `t` in seconds, `v` the value, `ease` a name (`in_out_cubic`, `out_expo`, `out_back`, `spring`...) or a CSS-style bezier `{"bezier": [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1]}`. `repeat`: `cycle` or `pingpong`.
  * **Drivers** : `wiggle`, `oscillate`, and `audio`, which follows a soundtrack band so a param pulses with the music.
  * **Expressions** : `{"expr": "..."}`, a formula of `t`, with a list for vectors.

## timing

```
"timing": { "in": 2, "out": 6, "offset": 2, "speed": 0.5 }
``` 

  * `in`, `out`: when the node is on screen. Outside its window a composite passes its background through and an effect passes its source; neither costs anything.
  * `offset`: where the node's local time zero sits in its parent's time. `speed`: local seconds per parent second (negative plays backwards). `loop`: local time wraps at this duration.
  * Windows compose through nesting. For cuts between shots, prefer `transition` nodes (crossfade, dip, wipe, push, slide, iris, zoom, dissolve, glitch, blur); each shot renders only while it is on screen.

## components

A component is a small document with its own params and inputs, used like an op. `"$name"` inside a component refers to one of its params. Components are flattened before planning, so they cost nothing at render time. `uf import-svg` and `uf import-lottie` write SVG artwork and Lottie animations as components with every part editable.

## Assets, colour, type

  * File paths (footage, images, fonts, SVG, Lottie, audio) are relative to the document.
  * Colours are sRGB hex (`#ff48b0`, `#ff48b080`) or 0–1 arrays with straight alpha. Compositing is in linear light; set `"space": "srgb"` on an `over`, `blend` or `gradient` to blend the way CSS and Figma do.
  * Fonts: a family name (any Google Font is fetched once by name), a font file, or a bundled face (`ultrafast:display`, `ultrafast:sans`, `ultrafast:serif`, `ultrafast:mono`, `ultrafast:wide`). Variable fonts animate any axis with `axis_<tag>`.

## Schema and versions

Documents carry `"version": 1`. The JSON Schema is published at [ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json](<https://ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json>) for editor completion and validation; `uf schema` prints the same file, and `uf ops` the vocabulary with every param's type and default. Changes within a version are additive.


---

# Render video from JSON: a worked example · ultrafast

# Render video from JSON.

One JSON file in, a finished video out, rendered on your GPU. A worked example, then the same document from the command line, over HTTP, from Python or TypeScript, and once per row of a spreadsheet.

## A whole video in 21 lines

A 6-second title card at 1920×1080: a moving marble background, darkened, a title whose letters rise into place from the centre out, a subtitle that types itself on, then bloom and film grain. It is the engine's `title` starter (`uf new title card.json`) with its two lines of text changed.

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "format": { "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "fps": 30, "duration": 6, "motion_blur": { "samples": 6, "shutter": 0.5 } },
  "output": "finish",
  "nodes": {
    "world": { "op": "marble", "params": { "filaments": 0.6 } },
    "dim": { "op": "adjust", "inputs": { "source": "world" }, "params": { "exposure": -1.2 } },
    "title": { "op": "text", "params": { "text": "Night Shift", "font": "Geist", "weight": 700, "size": 200, "align": "center", "valign": "middle",
      "position": [960, 520], "color": "#ffffff", "tracking": -6,
      "stagger": 0.05, "stagger_order": "center",
      "glyph_offset": { "keys": [ { "t": 0.3, "v": [0, 80], "ease": { "bezier": [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1] } }, { "t": 1.1, "v": [0, 0] } ] },
      "glyph_opacity": { "keys": [ { "t": 0.3, "v": 0 }, { "t": 0.6, "v": 1 } ] } } },
    "sub": { "op": "text", "params": { "text": "Episode 41 · out Thursday", "font": "Geist", "size": 44, "align": "center", "valign": "middle",
      "position": { "wiggle": { "frequency": 0.4, "amplitude": [6, 4], "base": [960, 660] } }, "color": "#ffffffb0", "tracking": 2,
      "reveal": { "keys": [ { "t": 1.0, "v": 0 }, { "t": 2.2, "v": 30 } ] } } },
    "l1": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "title", "bg": "dim" } },
    "l2": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "sub", "bg": "l1" } },
    "lit": { "op": "bloom", "inputs": { "source": "l2" }, "params": { "intensity": 0.5 } },
    "finish": { "op": "grain", "inputs": { "source": "lit" } }
  }
}
``` 

[Video: The title card the JSON describes: Night Shift rises letter by letter over moving marble, then Episode 41, out Thursday types on](https://ultrafast.mov/media/guides/json-card.mp4) card.json, exported. About 0.7 s from the command to the finished MP4 on one RTX 5090, and `uf review` found nothing to fix.

Four parts make every document:

  * `format`: size, frame rate, length, and motion blur (here 6 samples over half a frame's shutter).
  * `nodes`: a graph. Each node has an `op` (one of 70), its `params`, and `inputs` naming other nodes. Generators such as `marble` and `text` have none; `over` takes a foreground and a background; effects take a `source`.
  * Animated params: any param can be a constant, a list of keyframes, a driver such as `wiggle`, or a formula of `t`.
  * `output`: the node whose picture is the video.

There is no timeline of tracks. A node is on screen when its `timing` says so (all of the film when it has none), and layering is the order of `over` nodes. The full shape is in [the document reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>), and every op with its params is in [the op reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/>).

## Check, look, export

```
curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh    # or: brew install ultrafastmov/tap/ultrafast
uf check card.json                                  # {"ok": true, "issues": []} before anything renders
uf sheet card.json --count 9 --out sheet.png        # nine labelled frames on one image
uf review card.json                                 # every frame read for unreadable, clipped or too-brief text
uf export card.json card.mp4                        # H.264 MP4; the container follows the file name
``` 

`check` catches an unknown op or param, an input that points at no node, or a malformed colour before any GPU work, and names the node for each. `sheet` renders a few frames to one image, which is how an agent or a person sees the motion without watching it. `export` writes MP4 (H.264, HEVC or AV1), MOV (ProRes up to 4444 XQ, with alpha), WebM, GIF, PNG or EXR sequences, or the sound alone, at any size and frame rate:

```
uf export card.json card.mov --codec prores --prores-profile 4444 --alpha   # a transparent master
uf export card.json card-4k.mp4 --size 4k --codec hevc
uf export card.json card.gif --size 720p
``` 

Rendering runs on the GPU: Metal on a Mac with Apple silicon, Vulkan on Linux. The same document renders the same picture on every machine: fonts come with the engine or are fetched by name, and the GPU kernels are the same everywhere. Without a GPU, the Docker image renders on the CPU, much more slowly.

## Animation

The example uses three of the five ways to set a param. Keyframes move the letters (`glyph_offset` and `glyph_opacity`, staggered 0.05 s apart from the centre), a driver keeps the subtitle drifting (`wiggle`), and keyframes on `reveal` type it on.

```
"size": 64
"position": { "keys": [ { "t": 0, "v": [540, 2100], "ease": "out_expo" }, { "t": 0.8, "v": [540, 960] } ] }
"rotation": { "keys": [ { "t": 0, "v": 0 }, { "t": 1, "v": 10 } ], "repeat": "pingpong" }
"position": { "wiggle": { "frequency": 2, "amplitude": 10, "base": [540, 960] } }
"opacity":  { "expr": "0.5 + 0.5 * sin(t * 3)" }
``` 

Eases are named (`in_out_cubic`, `out_back`, `spring`...) or a CSS-style bezier. An `audio` driver makes a param follow a band of the soundtrack. To show a node only part of the time, give it `"timing": { "in": 2, "out": 6 }`.

## One video per row

Columns named `node.param` set that param in each row; other columns fill the output name. Three episode cards from one document:

```
name,title.text,sub.text
ep41,Night Shift,Episode 41 · out Thursday
ep42,Night Shift,Episode 42 · out 4 December
ep43,Night Shift,Episode 43 · out 11 December
``` 

```
uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4'     # one warm renderer, a video per row
uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --docs docs/               # or write each row's document and render later
``` 

The subtitle's `reveal` runs to 30 glyphs, so the longest row's 28 type on in full. A reveal counts glyphs, so give it room for the longest row's text.

Rows can be CSV, JSON or JSON lines, and a column can change the format too (`format.width`, `format.height`), so one sheet can give several sizes; frame-relative layout such as blocks and captions follows the frame.

## Over HTTP and from code

`uf serve` is the same engine behind an HTTP API with one API key, on your own GPU. Short renders come back in the response; longer ones are stored with a signed link.

```
docker run --gpus all -p 8080:8080 -v ultrafast:/data ghcr.io/ultrafastmov/ultrafast:latest serve

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/render -H "Authorization: Bearer $ULTRAFAST_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"document": '"$(cat card.json)"', "output": {"codec": "h264", "size": "1080p", "inline": true}}' -o card.mp4
``` 

The Python and TypeScript SDKs wrap the same API, with no dependencies:

```
from ultrafastmov import Ultrafast

uf = Ultrafast()                      # the server on this machine; ULTRAFAST_API_KEY
doc = uf.load("card.json")
for issue in uf.review(doc):
    print(issue.kind, issue.node, issue.message)
uf.render(doc).save("card.mp4")
``` 

```
import { Ultrafast } from "ultrafastmov";

const uf = new Ultrafast();
const doc = await uf.load("card.json");
await (await uf.render(doc)).save("card.mp4");
``` 

Endpoints for checking, single frames, contact sheets, reviews and uploads are in the [HTTP API reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>).

## From an agent

A JSON document is a good thing for a coding agent to write: it is short, it can be checked before anything renders, and the agent can look at the frames it made. With the skill installed, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI know the format and the loop; the MCP server gives any MCP client the same tools without a shell.

```
npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast        # the skill
claude mcp add ultrafast -- uf mcp           # 20 MCP tools, local
``` 

Measured on the same 10-second short, the ultrafast document took about 1,234 output tokens, against 1,868 for the same video in Remotion and 1,680 in HyperFrames ([method](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>)). More on the [video MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/mcp/>) page.

## The schema

The document format is versioned (`"version": 1`) and published as JSON Schema at [ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json](<https://ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json>). Point your editor at it for completion and inline errors:

```
{ "$schema": "https://ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json", "version": 1, "format": { }, "nodes": { }, "output": "finish" }
``` 

The schema checks shape; `uf check` also checks meaning: that ops and params exist, inputs point at real nodes, values are well formed, and shaders compile.

## Other JSON video formats

Several tools describe a video as JSON. What each one's docs say, as of 23 November 2026:

Format| Shape| Where it renders  
---|---|---  
ultrafast document| a graph of nodes with animated params and timing windows; 3D, shaders and simulations are nodes| your GPU, locally or with `uf serve`; open source  
[Shotstack Edit](<https://shotstack.io/docs/api/>)| a timeline of tracks of clips; 16 asset types; merge fields for templates| Shotstack's cloud  
[JSON2Video Movie](<https://json2video.com/docs/v2/reference/json-syntax>)| scenes that play back to back, each with elements; variables, conditions and iteration| JSON2Video's cloud  
[Creatomate RenderScript](<https://creatomate.com/docs/api/render-script/element-properties>)| elements on tracks with keyframes; nested compositions| Creatomate's cloud  
[Editly](<https://github.com/mifi/editly#readme>)| a JSON5 edit spec of clips and layers| locally with Node.js and FFmpeg; open source  
[VideoFlow](<https://github.com/ybouane/VideoFlow#readme>)| TypeScript compiled to a portable JSON format| headless Chromium on a server, or WebCodecs in the browser; open source  
  
The hosted services are compared in more depth on [ultrafast vs JSON-to-video APIs](<https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/json-to-video-api/>), and the open-source tools on [Remotion alternatives](<https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/remotion/>).

# Personalized videos from a CSV, open source · ultrafast

> Make one personalized video per row of a CSV or JSON file on your own GPU with an open-source engine: the template, the sheet, checking every row before rendering, long names, a photo per row, and the same from Python or HTTP.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/

Docs

# Personalized videos from a CSV.

A template and a spreadsheet make a finished video per row, each with its own customer name, order number and code. Rendered on your own GPU by an open-source engine, so the rows never leave your machine and no one charges per video.

## Start

  * [Quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)
  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

## Guides

  * [Render video from JSON](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/render-video-from-json/>)
  * [Personalized videos from a CSV](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/>)
  * [Make a video with Claude Code](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/claude-code/>)
  * [Lottie to MP4, WebM or ProRes](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/lottie-to-mp4/>)

## Reference

  * [Ops](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/>)
  * [CLI](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>)
  * [MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>)
  * [HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>)

## For agents

  * [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>)
  * [This page as Markdown](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/index.md>)

[Video: Twelve thank-you videos playing side by side, each with its own name, colour, order number and discount code](https://ultrafast.mov/media/guides/csv-batch.mp4) Twelve of 100 videos made from one template and a 100-row sheet. All 100 exported in 18.0 s on one RTX 5090. **On this page**

  1. The template
  2. The sheet
  3. Check every row first
  4. Long names
  5. Render the batch
  6. A photo or clip per row
  7. From code, a queue or an agent
  8. Limits
  9. Questions

## The template

The template is an ordinary ultrafast document: a JSON file with a `format`, a graph of `nodes` and an `output` (the whole shape is in [Render video from JSON](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/render-video-from-json/>)). This one is the engine's vertical starter (`uf new vertical card.json`), a 6-second 1080×1920 card, with its words changed to a thank-you note. Three of its nodes are the parts that change per customer:

```
"line2": { "op": "text", "params": {
  "text": "Priya.", "font": "Instrument Serif", "style": "italic", "size": 190, "color": "#ffd7a8",
  "position": { "keys": [ { "t": 0.55, "v": [84, 1210], "ease": { "bezier": [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1] } },
                          { "t": 1.25, "v": [84, 1020] } ] } } },
"label": { "op": "text", "params": {
  "text": "ORDER 10482", "font": "Geist Mono", "size": 26, "position": [86, 600] } },
"code": { "op": "text", "params": {
  "text": "10% off the next one: PRIYA10", "font": "Geist Mono", "size": 36, "color": "#ffd7a8",
  "position": [86, 1320], "reveal": { "keys": [ { "t": 2.4, "v": 0 }, { "t": 4.4, "v": 50 } ] } } }
``` 

Nothing in the template marks a field as a variable. Any param of any node can be set from the sheet, so the design stays a normal document you can preview, check and edit like any other.

## The sheet

A column named `node.param` sets that param in each row's copy of the template. Any other column is just data, and can name the output file.

```
name,line2.text,label.text,code.text,line2.color
priya,Priya.,ORDER 10482,10% off the next one: PRIYA10,#ffd7a8
tomas,Tomás.,ORDER 10483,10% off the next one: TOMAS10,#a8e0ff
mei,Mei.,ORDER 10484,10% off the next one: MEI10,#c8ffa8
``` 

  * Rows can be CSV, a JSON array of objects, or JSON lines.
  * Numbers are read as numbers (`line2.size` = `160`), colours as hex text with optional alpha.
  * `format.width`, `format.height` and the other format fields can be columns too. Layout built from blocks and captions follows the frame; pixel positions such as this card's don't, so give each size its own template.
  * In `--out`, `{name}` is filled from the `name` column (any column works) and `{row}` is the row number. Two rows that would write the same file stop the batch before it starts (`Error: row 97: writes out/ines.mp4 again`, from an Inès and an Ines), so add `{row}` when names can repeat.

## Check every row before anything renders

`uf batch` builds every row's document first and checks each one, so a typo in row 400 stops the run before the first frame. The error names the row and what's wrong:

```
$ uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4'
Error: row 1: `nosuch.text`: no node `nosuch` (did you mean `code`?)
``` 

To see each row's document, write them out instead of rendering, and check them like any other file:

```
uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4' --docs docs/   # docs/priya.json, docs/tomas.json, docs/mei.json
for f in docs/*.json; do uf check "$f"; done
``` 

`check` reports two levels. A missing file is an error (`"severity": "error"`) and stops a batch. A value of the wrong type, such as text in a number column, is a warning: the batch still runs, so read the warnings when a sheet comes from somewhere new.

## Long names

Add a row for `Maximiliana-Josefina.` and `check` still passes: a name too wide for the frame is a valid document. Catching it takes a render. `uf sheet` puts nine frames of one row on a single image, and `uf review` reads every frame for text that is clipped, overlapping, too small or on screen too briefly to read:

```
uf sheet docs/maximiliana.json --count 9 --out sheet.png
uf review docs/maximiliana.json --safe social      # also flags text under a social app's buttons and captions
``` 

For a sheet of unknown names, review the longest few rows before the full run. For full names with spaces, a wrap width (`"width"` on the text node, in pixels) breaks a long one onto a second line instead of running it off the edge.

Text that types itself on needs the same care. `reveal` counts glyphs, so its last key must be at least as long as the longest row's text. This card's code first stopped at 30, and `10% off the next one: ISABELA10`, 31 glyphs, ended on `ISABELA1`. Neither `check` nor `review` reports a reveal that stops short, so the card now types on at the same speed up to 50, and the sheet of the longest row is the place to see it.

## Render the batch

```
uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4'
uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4' --codec hevc --quality high   # export settings apply to every row
``` 

One renderer stays warm for the whole sheet, so fonts and GPU pipelines load once for the whole run, not once per video. Each row prints its frame count and time, and the run ends with the total. With this card and a 100-row sheet, on one RTX 5090 workstation:

```
$ uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4'
1/100 out/priya.mp4: 180 frames in 0.33 s
2/100 out/tomas.mp4: 180 frames in 0.18 s
3/100 out/mei.mp4: 180 frames in 0.18 s
...
100 videos in 18.0 s
``` 

That's 18.0 s for 100 six-second 1080×1920 videos, the same in each of three runs. After the first row, each video took 0.17 or 0.18 s. A longer or busier template takes longer per row. Every export setting works here: H.264, HEVC or AV1 MP4, ProRes, WebM, GIF, any size and frame rate. `uf estimate card.json` reports the GPU time of one video before you start.

## A photo, a logo or a clip per row

An `image` or `video` node takes its file from `src`, so a column can swap it per row:

```
name,line2.text,photo.src
priya,Priya.,photos/priya.jpg
tomas,Tomás.,photos/tomas.jpg
``` 

Relative paths resolve from the template's folder. If you write the row documents somewhere else with `--docs`, use absolute paths in the sheet so each document still finds its files. A row whose file is missing fails the check, before rendering starts.

## From code, a queue or an agent

When the rows come from a database or a form instead of a file, set the params in code. `uf serve` runs the same engine behind an HTTP API on your machine, with one API key, and the Python and TypeScript SDKs wrap it:

```
import csv
from ultrafastmov import Ultrafast

uf = Ultrafast()                          # your uf serve; ULTRAFAST_API_KEY
card = uf.load("card.json")
for row in csv.DictReader(open("customers.csv")):
    doc = card.copy()                     # a deep copy; relative paths still resolve from card.json's folder
    doc["nodes"]["line2"]["params"]["text"] = row["first_name"] + "."
    doc["nodes"]["code"]["params"]["text"] = f"10% off the next one: {row['code']}"
    uf.render(doc).save(f"out/{row['id']}.mp4")
``` 

Any tool that can send an HTTP request can do the same with `POST /v1/render` and the row's document ([HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>)). A self-hosted server renders one job at a time on its GPU; send the rows one after another. Agents get the same thing as an MCP tool: `ultrafast_batch` renders one document per row of a data file, or of rows passed inline (up to 20 a call on a remote server, a download link per row; see [MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>)).

## Limits

  * It needs a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU. Without a GPU, the Docker image renders on the CPU, correctly but much more slowly.
  * There's no hosted service yet: you run the renderer. [ultrafast Cloud](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>) is a waitlist.
  * One template per batch. Different layouts per segment are separate templates, or a `format` column with layout that follows the frame.
  * Hosted APIs such as Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate run the render for you and charge per minute; their prices and formats are compared on [ultrafast vs JSON-to-video APIs](<https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/json-to-video-api/>).

## Questions

Can I make personalized videos from a spreadsheet for free?

Yes, if you have the hardware. ultrafast is open source (Apache-2.0 or MIT) and renders on your own Mac with Apple silicon or Linux machine with a Vulkan GPU, so there is no per-video or per-minute fee: `uf batch card.json --data rows.csv --out 'out/{name}.mp4'` makes one video per row.

Does my customer data leave my machine?

Not with the command line: `uf batch` reads the sheet and renders on the same machine. With `uf serve`, the rows go only to the server you run. Fonts named in a template may be downloaded by name the first time they are used.

Can each row have its own photo or video clip?

Yes. A column such as `photo.src` sets the file of an `image` or `video` node per row. Relative paths resolve from the template's folder, and a row whose file is missing stops the batch before anything renders.

How do I stop long names from running off the frame?

Render and look: `uf review` on the longest rows reports text that runs off the frame, overlaps other text or is too small, and `uf sheet` shows nine frames on one image. A wrap width on the text node breaks a long full name onto a second line. `uf check` alone can't see it, because a long name is a valid document.

How long does it take to render 100 personalized videos?

It depends on the template and the GPU. The 6-second 1080×1920 card in this guide took 18.0 s for a 100-row sheet on one RTX 5090 workstation, about 0.18 s per video after the first. `uf estimate card.json` reports one video's GPU time on your machine before you run the batch.

Can I do this from n8n, Zapier or my own code?

From your own code, yes: the Python and TypeScript SDKs talk to `uf serve`, so you copy the template, set the params from your data and render. There is no n8n or Zapier node, but their HTTP request step can POST each row's document to `/v1/render` on your server.

# Make a video with Claude Code: a real session · ultrafast

> Make videos with Claude Code and ultrafast: install the plugin, the exact prompt, every tool call the agent made, the contact sheets it looked at, an edit by asking, and the time and tokens it took.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/guides/claude-code/

Docs

# Make a video with Claude Code.

Claude Code can make real videos when it has a video engine to write for. Here is one session from start to finish: a 10-second vertical video for a coffee roastery, from the prompt to the MP4, with every tool call it made, what it looked at, the edit after, and how long each part took.

[Video: A 10-second vertical video: NOW OPEN, Third Crack, Roasted on Thursdays, 14 Mill Lane, Thursday to Sunday, 8 to 2, in cream and amber type on a warm brown background](https://ultrafast.mov/media/guides/claude-code-third-crack.mp4) Made by Claude Code with ultrafast from the two prompts on this page: 53.1 s for the first version, 31.2 s for the edit. **On this page**

  10. Questions

## Install

Two parts: `uf`, the engine that renders on your GPU, and the ultrafast plugin for Claude Code, which brings the skill (how to write and check a video document) and the MCP server (`uf mcp`, the tools Claude calls).

```
curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh        # or: brew install ultrafastmov/tap/ultrafast
claude plugin marketplace add ultrafastmov/ultrafast
claude plugin install ultrafast@ultrafast
``` 

It runs on a Mac with Apple silicon or on Linux with a Vulkan GPU. To confirm Claude Code can reach the engine:

```
$ claude mcp list
plugin:ultrafast:ultrafast: uf mcp - ✔ Connected
``` 

Without the plugin, the same two parts install separately: `npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast` for the skill and `claude mcp add ultrafast -- uf mcp` for the server. The session below used that route, in an empty folder with no other settings, so nothing else on the machine shaped the result.

## The prompt

One message, sent as written:

```
Make a 10-second vertical video (1080x1920) announcing the opening of a small coffee roastery
called Third Crack: its name, the line "Roasted on Thursdays", and the address 14 Mill Lane.
Warm, slow and confident. Check it, look at the frames, fix anything the review finds, and
export an MP4.
``` 

The last sentence names the loop the skill teaches: check the document, look at frames, review every frame, then export.

## What Claude did

Every step below is a tool call from the session's log, in order, with what came back.

  1. **Loaded the ultrafast skill** and asked `ultrafast_ops` for the parameters of the ops it planned to use: `gradient`, `noise`, `text`, `shape`, `over`, `vignette` and `grain`.
  2. **Wrote`third-crack.json`** in one go: a radial brown gradient, slow noise drifting upward as smoke, five layers of type and a thin rule, each with its own timing, then a vignette and film grain. The name rises in letter by letter: 

```
"name": { "op": "text", "params": {
  "text": "Third\nCrack", "font": "Fraunces", "weight": 600, "size": 190, "line_height": 0.98,
  "color": "#f3e6d3", "align": "center", "valign": "middle", "position": [540, 860],
  "stagger": 0.08,
  "glyph_opacity": { "keys": [{ "t": 0.9, "v": 0, "ease": "in_out_sine" }, { "t": 2.1, "v": 1 }] },
  "glyph_offset": { "keys": [{ "t": 0.9, "v": [0, 36], "ease": { "bezier": [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1] } }, { "t": 2.4, "v": [0, 0] }] } } }
``` 

  3. **Fixed its own slip.** It had given the tagline two `position` keys, a fixed one and an animated one, and deleted the fixed one before going on.
  4. **`ultrafast_check`** on the document, without rendering: `{"issues": []}`.
  5. **`ultrafast_sheet`** : eight frames from 0.5 s to 9.9 s on one image, which Claude looked at. Its note: "Looks right: warm, centered, everything spelled correctly."
  6. **`ultrafast_review`** with `"safe": "social"`, which reads every frame for clipped, overlapping, low-contrast, too-small or too-brief text and for text under a social app's buttons: `{"frames": 300, "issues": [], "seconds": 2.02, "texts": 4}`.
  7. **`ultrafast_frame`** at 9 s, to see the finished card at full size.
  8. **`ultrafast_export`** : `exported 300 frames (1080x1920 @ 30 fps, mp4 h264, high) in 0.36 s (823 fps)`.
  9. **Checked the file** with `ffprobe` (H.264, 1080×1920, 30 fps, 10.0 s, 1.7 MB) and summed up, including one choice it made on its own: "I added "NOW OPEN" myself to make it read as an opening announcement, so remove it if you'd rather keep to just the three lines you gave me."

![Contact sheet of eight frames from 0.5 to 9.9 seconds: NOW OPEN fades in, Third Crack rises in letter by letter, a rule draws under it, then Roasted on Thursdays and 14 Mill Lane fade in on a warm brown background.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/guides/claude-code-sheet-1.webp) The contact sheet Claude looked at before the review, as `ultrafast_sheet` returned it.

## When the review finds something

This draft passed the review on the first try, so there was nothing to fix. Drafts often don't. The first draft of the pottery class teaser on the [home page](<https://ultrafast.mov/#agents>) came back with eight findings, among them:

```
clipped        "Pottery class" runs off the frame (right by 40 px)
low contrast   "HALDEN CLAY STUDIO" never reaches readable contrast (best 1.6:1, want 3:1 or more)
too brief      "First class free" is readable for 0.4 s; 3 words need about 0.9 s
flashing       more than 3 flashes per second: a photosensitive seizure risk (WCAG 2.3.1)
``` 

Each finding names the text and the problem, so Claude can fix the document and run the review again until it comes back empty. That loop is why to ask for it: the agent sees its own mistakes before you do.

## Changing it by asking

A second message, in the same session:

```
Make the address a little bigger, and add a line under it: Thursday to Sunday, 8 to 2.
Then check, review and export again.
``` 

Claude didn't rewrite the file. It sent `ultrafast_edit` ten changes in one call: it made the address larger, added the new line as a node and wired it into the picture, and moved the other lines up by about 40 px to keep the block centred. Five of the ten:

```
{ "edit": "set_param", "node": "address", "param": "size", "value": 50 },
{ "edit": "set_param", "node": "address", "param": "position", "value": [540, 1255] },
{ "edit": "add_node", "id": "hours", "node": { "op": "text", "params": {
    "text": "Thursday to Sunday, 8 to 2", "font": "DM Mono", "size": 34, "color": "#e8c79a",
    "align": "center", "valign": "middle", "position": [540, 1330] } } },
{ "edit": "add_node", "id": "c6", "node": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "hours", "bg": "c5" } } },
{ "edit": "connect", "node": "vig", "port": "source", "source": "c6" }
``` 

The check passed. Then the contact sheet showed something the check couldn't: "The hours line sits a bit tight under the address, so I'll give it a little more room before reviewing." A second edit moved it down 15 px and set it 2 px larger. The review read all 300 frames and 5 texts with no findings, and the export took 0.37 s.

![Contact sheet of the edited video, eight frames from 1.4 to 9.9 seconds: the address is larger and a line reading Thursday to Sunday, 8 to 2 fades in under it.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/guides/claude-code-sheet-2.webp) The sheet after the edit, where Claude saw the new line sitting too close to the address.

## Time and tokens

Wall time runs from starting Claude Code to its exit, so it includes start-up, every model turn and every tool call.

| First video| The edit  
---|---|---  
Wall time| 53.1 s| 31.2 s  
Model turns| 15| 10  
Output tokens| 4,719| 2,597  
Review| 300 frames, 0 issues, 2.0 s| 300 frames, 0 issues, 1.8 s  
Export| 0.36 s| 0.37 s  
Cost at API list prices| $0.46| $0.67  
  
Claude Code 2.1.325 with Claude Opus 5.5 and ultrafast 0.2.0; both exports took under 0.4 s on one RTX 5090 workstation. The costs are what Claude Code reported at API list prices. On a Pro or Max plan the session counts toward the plan's usage instead. Most of the wall time is the model thinking and writing; the engine's share, from check to export, was a few seconds per turn.

## Prompts to try

Each of these briefs made one of the films on the [examples page](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/>), where the document behind each one is published:

  * "A 10-second vertical teaser for my pottery class. Saturdays, first class free."
  * "Turn NOAA's Mauna Loa CO₂ file into a chart for Instagram."
  * "Show how Artemis I got to the Moon and back, from NASA's trajectory data."
  * "Make every member their year in review from this spreadsheet."
  * "A 15-second loop for the album cover: something growing, in celadon."

Say what it's for, how long, the size, and the words that must appear. Give Claude the files it should use (footage, a logo, a data file) by path. For one video per row of a spreadsheet, see [Personalized videos from a CSV](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/>).

## If it doesn't work

  * **`✘ Failed to connect — ENOENT: Executable not found in $PATH: "uf"`** in `claude mcp list`: the plugin is installed but Claude Code was started without `uf` on its PATH. Open a new terminal after installing, or add the folder the installer printed to your PATH, then start Claude Code again.
  * **Which GPU will it use?** `uf info` names the GPU it will render on. ultrafast needs one: Apple silicon on a Mac, or a Vulkan GPU on Linux.
  * **Fonts.** The session used Fraunces and DM Mono by name. Fonts named in a document may be downloaded by name the first time they're used, so the first render with a new font needs a network connection.
  * **Claude doesn't use the tools.** Check that the plugin is enabled (`claude plugin list`) and name the loop in the prompt: "check it, look at the frames, review it, then export".

## Remotion, HyperFrames and other agents

Claude Code also makes video with Remotion (React rendered in headless Chrome) and HyperFrames (HTML and GSAP in headless Chrome). On one RTX 5090, the same three 10-second videos exported in 0.66–0.78 s with ultrafast; Remotion took 3.1–8.6 times as long at its fastest settings, and HyperFrames 4.6–5.7 times ([benchmark](<https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/>)). For the same 10-second short, the ultrafast document took about 1,234 output tokens against 1,868 for Remotion. Head-to-head pages: [ultrafast vs Remotion](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/remotion/>), [ultrafast vs HyperFrames](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/hyperframes/>). For every way Claude can make video, including Claude Motion, see [Can Claude make videos?](<https://ultrafast.mov/learn/can-claude-make-videos/>)

The same skill and MCP server work in Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and any MCP client: setup for each is on [Integrations](<https://ultrafast.mov/integrations/>), and the tools are listed in [MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>).

## Questions

Can Claude Code make videos?

Yes, with a video engine to write for. With the ultrafast plugin, Claude Code writes the video as a JSON document, checks it, looks at its frames, reviews every frame and exports an MP4 on your GPU. In the session on this page that took 53.1 s from the prompt to a 10-second 1080×1920 MP4.

What do I need to install?

The `uf` engine (`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` or Homebrew) and the plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add ultrafastmov/ultrafast`, then `claude plugin install ultrafast@ultrafast`. It renders on a Mac with Apple silicon or on Linux with a Vulkan GPU.

How many tokens does a video take?

In this session, 4,719 output tokens for the first 10-second video and 2,597 for an edit, with Claude Opus 5.5. A longer or busier video takes more. Measured on the same 10-second short, an ultrafast document was about 1,234 output tokens against 1,868 for Remotion.

Does Claude Code see the video it makes?

It sees frames. `ultrafast_sheet` returns several frames on one image and `ultrafast_frame` one frame at full size, and `ultrafast_review` reads all of them for clipped, low-contrast, overlapping, too-small or too-brief text. In this session Claude spotted a line sitting too close to another on a contact sheet and moved it before exporting.

Can I edit the video after it's made?

Yes, by asking in the same session. Claude changes the document with `ultrafast_edit` (set a param, add or remove a node, rewire) instead of rewriting it, then checks, reviews and exports again. The edit on this page took 31.2 s.

Does it work on Windows?

Through WSL2 on a machine with a Vulkan GPU. There is no native Windows build.

# Lottie to MP4, transparent WebM or ProRes 4444 on your GPU · ultrafast

> Convert Lottie JSON to MP4, transparent WebM, ProRes 4444, GIF or PNG frames with one open-source command on your own GPU: measured times, a whole folder at once, recolouring, and how closely it matches lottie-web across 217 files.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/guides/lottie-to-mp4/

Docs

# Lottie to MP4, WebM or ProRes.

Turn a Lottie JSON file into an MP4, a transparent WebM, ProRes 4444, a GIF or PNG frames with one command, rendered on your own GPU by an open-source engine. The animation comes in as vector paths, so it stays sharp at 4K and every colour in it can be changed.

## Start

  * [Quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)
  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

  * [Make a video with Claude Code](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/claude-code/>)

[Video: Three vertical panels: the Lottie logo animation on teal, the same animation in ink and orange on cream, and a second Lottie animation of teal strokes over a checkerboard that shows its transparent background](https://ultrafast.mov/media/guides/lottie-to-mp4.mp4) Two Lottie files from lottie-android (Apache-2.0), in one ultrafast render: as designed, recoloured with one jq command, and with its transparent background kept. **On this page**

  1. Convert one file

  9. Questions

## Convert one file

Install `uf` (a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU; Windows through WSL2):

```
curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh     # or: brew install ultrafastmov/tap/ultrafast
``` 

ultrafast renders documents, so the Lottie goes into a short one: a frame size, a frame rate, a length, and a `lottie` node pointing at the file.

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "format": { "width": 1080, "height": 1920, "fps": 30, "duration": 5.967 },
  "output": "logo",
  "nodes": {
    "logo": { "op": "lottie", "params": { "src": "lottie-logo.json", "size": [1080, 1920], "loop": false } }
  }
}
``` 

```
$ uf export logo.json logo.mp4
exported 179 frames (1080x1920 @ 30 fps, mp4 h264, standard) in 0.15 s = 1167 fps, 0 readbacks -> logo.mp4
``` 

  * `duration` is the Lottie's frame count over its frame rate: its `op` minus `ip`, divided by `fr`. This file has 179 frames at 30 fps, so 5.967 s.
  * `size` fits the animation into a box, keeping its proportions. The paths are drawn again at that size, not scaled up from pixels, so a 375×667 animation is as sharp at 1080×1920 or 4K as at its own size.
  * `loop` is on by default and repeats the animation to fill a longer video; with `false` it plays once.
  * `uf check logo.json` lists anything in the file that won't import, before you render.

From pressing Enter to a finished file took 0.51 s warm, of which 0.15 s was the export itself and the rest was start-up.

## Every format from the same document

The output format follows the file name; flags set the codec, size and transparency. Times are wall clock from the command to the file, warm, on one RTX 5090 workstation with the published 0.2.0 binary. The first four rows export `logo.json` from above (5.967 s). The rest export `logo2.json`, the same document pointed at `lottie-logo-2.json` (12.6 s), whose background is transparent.

Output| Command| Time| File  
---|---|---|---  
MP4, H.264, 1080×1920| `uf export logo.json logo.mp4`| 0.51 s| 118 KB  
MP4, HEVC| `uf export logo.json logo.mp4 --codec hevc`| 0.50 s| 88 KB  
MP4, 4K (2160×3840)| `uf export logo.json logo-4k.mp4 --size 4k`| 1.2–1.3 s| 255 KB  
GIF, 540×960| `uf export logo.json logo.gif --size 540x960`| 1.3 s| 104 KB  
MP4, H.264, 12.6 s| `uf export logo2.json logo2.mp4`| 0.64 s| 1.5 MB  
ProRes 4444 with alpha| `uf export logo2.json logo2.mov --codec prores --alpha`| 3.6 s| 124 MB  
WebM (VP9) with alpha| `uf export logo2.json logo2.webm --alpha`| 6.1 s| 1.4 MB  
PNG frames with alpha| `uf export logo2.json 'frames/{frame:05}.png' --alpha`| 1.4–1.5 s| 378 files  
  
  * H.264 and HEVC are encoded on the GPU straight from the rendered frames. ProRes, VP9, GIF and PNG are encoded on the CPU, which is why they take longer. ProRes varied the most: a median of 3.6 s over six runs, between 3.4 and 8.3 s.
  * The transparent files are really transparent: the ProRes is 4444 with 12-bit alpha (`yuva444p12le`), and the WebM carries VP9's alpha channel. In a frame decoded from each, 85 % of the pixels are fully transparent. They drop into Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve or a web page.
  * `--fps 60` renders more frames between the Lottie's keyframes, and `--from` and `--to` export part of it. The full list is in the [CLI reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>).

## A whole folder of Lottie files

`uf batch` renders one video per row of a sheet, and each row can set the file, the size, the frame rate and the length. The template is the same short document, on white:

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "format": { "width": 512, "height": 512, "fps": 30, "duration": 3 },
  "output": "out",
  "nodes": {
    "bg": { "op": "solid", "params": { "color": "#ffffff" } },
    "anim": { "op": "lottie", "params": { "src": "anim.json", "loop": false } },
    "out": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "anim", "bg": "bg" } }
  }
}
``` 

A few lines of Python read each file's size, frame rate and length and write the sheet:

```
import csv, glob, json, os, sys

rows = []
for path in sorted(glob.glob("lottie/*.json")):
    a = json.load(open(path))
    scale = max(1, 512 / max(a["w"], a["h"]))           # draw small icons at 512 px or more
    w, h = round(a["w"] * scale / 2) * 2, round(a["h"] * scale / 2) * 2   # even sizes for H.264
    rows.append({"name": os.path.basename(path)[:-5], "anim.src": os.path.abspath(path),
                 "anim.size": json.dumps([w, h]), "format.width": w, "format.height": h,
                 "format.fps": a["fr"], "format.duration": (a["op"] - a["ip"]) / a["fr"]})
out = csv.DictWriter(sys.stdout, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
out.writeheader()
out.writerows(rows)
``` 

```
$ python3 rows.py > rows.csv
$ uf batch template.json --data rows.csv --out 'mp4/{name}.mp4'
1/208 mp4/AndroidWave.mp4: 123 frames in ...
...
208 videos in 35.6 s
``` 

That run converted 208 Lottie files from lottie-android's test set, 888 seconds of animation, in 35.6 s; the next two runs took 35.6 and 39.2 s. `uf batch` checks every row before it renders the first one, so a file that can't load stops the run with its row number instead of failing halfway. Swap `.mp4` for `.webm` and add `--alpha` (and drop the white `bg`) to get transparent files instead. How the sheet works is in [Personalized videos from a CSV](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/>).

## Change the colours, or anything else

The `lottie` node keeps the file as it is. To change it, `uf import-lottie` brings the animation into your document as ordinary nodes: every shape a `path` with its own colour, stroke, trim and keyframes, and every group and layer transform a `transform` node. The Lottie logo came in as 49 paths, 244 transforms, 47 `over` nodes that stack them, and a mask.

```
uf import-lottie lottie-logo.json --size 1080,1920 --name logo --into restyle.json
# then place it: { "op": "logo", "params": { "position": [0, 0] } }
``` 

The document is plain JSON, so a palette swap is one jq command. This is the one that made the middle panel of the clip above:

```
jq '(.components.logo.nodes[] | select(.op == "path") | .params.color) |=
  if . == [0, 0.82, 0.76, 1] then "#f3e9d6"
  elif . == [0, 0.48, 0.53, 1] then "#ff5a1f"
  elif . == [1, 1, 1, 1] or . == "#ffffff" then "#1d1a16"
  else . end' restyle.json > restyled.json
uf check restyled.json && uf export restyled.json restyled.mp4
``` 

A coding agent can make the same kind of change from a sentence ("make the teal background cream and the dark strokes orange"), because each colour, stroke width and keyframe is a field it can read and set. To look before exporting, `uf sheet restyled.json` puts nine frames on one image.

## Inside a longer video

A `lottie` node is a layer like any other. Give it a `position`, `scale` or `opacity`, put it over footage, a title or a background with an `over` node, and time it with a timing window. The clip at the top of this page is one document: two `lottie` nodes, the imported and recoloured copy, a checkerboard and three labels, exported in one pass.

```
"p1": { "op": "lottie", "params": { "src": "lottie-logo.json", "size": [315, 560], "position": [84, 60], "loop": false } },
"p3": { "op": "lottie", "params": { "src": "lottie-logo-2.json", "size": [315, 560], "position": [882, 60], "loop": false } },
"o1": { "op": "over", "inputs": { "fg": "p1", "bg": "bg" } }
``` 

Captions, music, a voiceover, grain and the rest of the engine's 70 ops work around it in the same render. The document format is in [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>).

## How close it is to lottie-web

ultrafast doesn't run lottie-web, the reference player. It reads the Lottie file itself and draws it with its own renderer, so the fair question is how often the two agree. To measure it, the 217 Lottie files in lottie-android's snapshot tests (its `lottiefiles` folder plus the four samples) were rendered at 10, 30, 50, 70 and 90 % of their length, by ultrafast 0.2.0 and by lottie-web 5.13.0's SVG renderer in headless Chromium, both on white at the file's own size. A pixel counts as different when any colour channel is off by more than 40 of 255.

![Three Lottie samples rendered by ultrafast in the top row and by lottie-web in the bottom row: the Lottie logo on teal, teal strokes from the second logo animation, and a purple arrow. The two rows look the same.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/guides/lottie-vs-lottie-web.webp) The three Apache-2.0 samples, middle frame. At their worst frame, 0.02 %, 0.77 % and 0.17 % of pixels differ.

Of 217 files| Files  
---|---  
Imported with no warnings| 103  
Didn't load: image files missing from the test set| 5  
Didn't load: a layer scaled to exactly 0 (see below)| 4  
Compared with lottie-web| 208  
… worst frame within 1 % of pixels| 113  
… within 2 %| 137  
… within 5 %| 165  
  
Files that import without warnings match more often: 89 of 99 are within 5 %, against 76 of the 109 files with warnings. Of the 43 files that differ by more than 5 %, 33 raised a warning when they were imported. These are the warnings in the set, with how many files raised each one:

Warning| Files| What you get instead  
---|---|---  
merge paths are not imported| 58| the shapes are drawn without being merged  
layer effects are not imported| 29| no After Effects effects (blurs, glows, fills)  
After Effects expressions are not run| 23| `loopOut`, `wiggle` and `time` run; other expressions keep their keyframes  
separated x/y position keys are merged| 14| x and y are keyed together at every key time of either, so the easing between keys can differ  
3D layers are flattened| 7| drawn flat  
time remapping is not imported| 7| the layer plays at its own speed  
gradient strokes use a solid stroke| 6| one colour  
mask modes other than add combine as add| 4| subtract and intersect masks add  
rounded corners on paths are not imported| 4| sharp corners  
skew is not imported| 3| no skew  
paragraph text boxes are set as point text| 3| no wrapping box  
animated gradient colours use their first key| 2| a still gradient  
  
Some differences come with no warning: 10 of the 99 warning-free files differ by more than 5 %. Two causes found in this test: a stroke with a width of 0, which lottie-web doesn't draw, is filled in the stroke's colour in 0.2.0; and a layer whose scale is keyed to exactly 0, a common way to pop something in, stops `uf check` and the render with `transform is not invertible (zero scale)`, naming the node.

To check your own file, run `uf check` on a document that uses it (it lists every warning), then look: `uf sheet logo.json` renders nine frames onto one image to compare with the file playing in a browser.

## If something looks wrong

  * **A .lottie file.** dotLottie files aren't read directly. A `.lottie` file is a zip archive: unzip it and point `src` at the JSON inside its `animations` folder.
  * **Missing images.** Images embedded in the JSON (base64) import as they are. Images the file links to are looked for next to the JSON, in the folder its asset names. `uf check` reports a missing one by path.
  * **Text in the wrong font.** Text layers use the family named in the file's font list: an installed font of that name, or else the Google Fonts family of that name, downloaded once. If it's neither, install the font, or change the family on the imported `text` node.
  * **A tiny frame fails to encode.** On NVIDIA GPUs, 0.2.0 can't encode H.264 at very small sizes such as 72×72. Render icons at 512 px or more; the paths stay sharp.
  * **Anything listed in the warnings above.** If the effect matters, fix it in the source file (expand the merge, bake the expression to keyframes) and export again from After Effects or your Lottie editor.
  * **No GPU.** The Docker image renders on the CPU through Mesa, correctly but much more slowly.

## Other ways to convert Lottie to video

  * **lottie-web in headless Chrome:** puppeteer-lottie, Remotion's `@remotion/lottie` and HyperFrames' Lottie converter play the file in the reference player and capture each frame from a browser page. Whatever lottie-web supports comes out as it does in a browser, and HyperFrames also reads dotLottie files. How browser capture compares with ultrafast on ordinary videos is in [Benchmarks](<https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/>).
  * **rlottie converters** , such as the ones made for Telegram stickers, write WebM, WebP or GIF.
  * **Upload sites** convert one file at a time in the browser, usually with a size limit and sometimes a sign-in.
  * **After Effects** itself, if you have the project the Lottie was exported from: render from the source and nothing is lost.

Use ultrafast when you want speed on your own machine, many files at once, ProRes 4444 or WebM with alpha from one command, the animation recoloured or edited before rendering, or the Lottie as one layer of a longer video. Use a lottie-web renderer when a file depends on effects, merge paths or expressions that ultrafast doesn't import, or when you need dotLottie support.

## Questions

How do I convert a Lottie JSON file to MP4?

Put the file in a short ultrafast document (a frame size, frame rate and length, and a `lottie` node whose `src` is the file), then run `uf export logo.json logo.mp4`. A 6-second 1080×1920 export took 0.51 s on an RTX 5090 workstation. The engine is open source and renders on your own Mac with Apple silicon or Linux machine with a Vulkan GPU.

Can I export a Lottie animation with a transparent background?

Yes. `uf export logo.json logo.mov --codec prores --alpha` writes ProRes 4444 with 12-bit alpha, `uf export logo.json logo.webm --alpha` writes VP9 WebM with alpha, and `'frames/{frame:05}.png' --alpha` writes transparent PNG frames. Leave out any background node so the empty parts stay transparent.

Does it read dotLottie (.lottie) files?

Not directly. A .lottie file is a zip archive: unzip it and point the `lottie` node at the JSON inside its `animations` folder.

Does the video look exactly like the Lottie in a browser?

Often, not always. ultrafast draws the file with its own renderer, not lottie-web. Across 208 files from lottie-android's test set, 113 had no frame with more than 1 % of pixels different from lottie-web and 165 were within 5 %. Merge paths, layer effects, most expressions, time remapping and 3D layers don't import, and `uf check` lists them for your file.

Can I convert a whole folder of Lottie files at once?

Yes: write a sheet with one row per file (its path, size, frame rate and length) and run `uf batch template.json --data rows.csv --out 'mp4/{name}.mp4'`. 208 files, 888 seconds of animation, took 35.6 s on one RTX 5090 workstation.

Can I change a Lottie's colours before rendering it?

Yes. `uf import-lottie` brings the animation into the document as ordinary nodes, each shape a path with its own colour, so a palette swap is a find-and-replace over the JSON (one jq command), or a sentence to a coding agent.

# MCP server

20 tools that let an agent write a video, look at it, fix it and export it, without a shell.

## Start

  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

  * [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>)
  * [This page as Markdown](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/index.md>)

**On this page**

  1. Local, over stdio
  2. Remote, over HTTP
  3. The tools
  4. How agents use them

## Local, over stdio

`uf mcp` is a stdio MCP server (JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line). Renders run on your GPU.

```
claude mcp add ultrafast -- uf mcp
``` 

```
[mcp_servers.ultrafast]
command = "uf"
args = ["mcp"]
``` 

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ultrafast": { "command": "uf", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
``` 

Documents stay plain JSON files. The server keeps a renderer per document, so repeated frames are fast, and reloads a file when it changes, whether the agent edits it with `ultrafast_edit` or writes it directly.

## Remote, over HTTP

`ultrafast serve` answers MCP over Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, with its API key as a bearer token, for agent frameworks and any client that can't run a local process. It serves the 16 tools that need no local files; they take the document and asset ids instead of file paths; frames and sheets come back as images and exports as download links.

```
claude mcp add --transport http ultrafast http://localhost:8080/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $ULTRAFAST_API_KEY"
``` 

A hosted server with OAuth sign-in, for the ChatGPT app and the Claude connector, comes with [ultrafast Cloud](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).

## The tools

tool| does  
---|---  
`ultrafast_ops`| The op vocabulary: ports, params, types, defaults, docs.  
`ultrafast_new`| Write a template (`vertical`, `title`, `square`, `promo`, `explainer`, `product`) to a path.  
`ultrafast_check`| Problems in a document, static and render-time.  
`ultrafast_frame`| One exact frame, returned as an image.  
`ultrafast_sheet`| A labelled contact sheet of frames, returned as an image.  
`ultrafast_review`| Renders the film and reports unreadable, too-brief, clipped, overlapping or tiny text, unsafe areas and seizure-risk flashing.  
`ultrafast_inspect`| What is on screen at a time: each element's node, bounds and words.  
`ultrafast_edit`| Apply an edit batch to the document file, atomically.  
`ultrafast_export`| Encode to MP4, MOV (ProRes), WebM, a GIF, a PNG or EXR sequence or sound alone, at any size, frame rate and quality level, transparent where the codec allows.  
`ultrafast_estimate`| Rendered minutes, GPU seconds and the time to the first byte, before rendering.  
`ultrafast_batch`| One document, a video per row of a CSV or JSON file.  
`ultrafast_profile`| GPU milliseconds per render group, for slow films.  
`ultrafast_beats`| Tempo, beats, downbeats and onsets of a soundtrack.  
`ultrafast_voiceover`| Speak a script to WAV with every word's time, for audio and captions.  
`ultrafast_import_svg`| An SVG as an editable component, or added to a document.  
`ultrafast_decompose`| A finished video as an editable document: plate, vector layers with their motion, gradients, type read back as text in its matched font.  
`ultrafast_match_font`| A text node's font, size, baseline, tracking and colour, from a video frame.  
`ultrafast_ocr`| The text in a video frame, with word boxes and a draft of text nodes.  
`ultrafast_measure`| Glyph metrics of a line of text.  
`ultrafast_outline`| A line of text as SVG path data.  
  
## How agents use them

  1. `ultrafast_new` or write the JSON; `ultrafast_ops` when unsure of a param.
  2. `ultrafast_check` until it's clean.
  3. `ultrafast_sheet` to see the motion; `ultrafast_inspect` to find the node behind a pixel.
  4. `ultrafast_review`; fix what it reports with `ultrafast_edit`.
  5. `ultrafast_export`.

The [MCP server overview](<https://ultrafast.mov/mcp/>) shows this loop on a real film, with the clients tested and how it differs from other video MCP servers.

The ultrafast skill teaches agents the document and this loop: `npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast`. In Claude Code, the plugin brings the skill and `uf mcp` together: `claude plugin marketplace add ultrafastmov/ultrafast`, then `claude plugin install ultrafast@ultrafast`.

Agents that read docs can start from [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>); every page here is also available as Markdown at `index.md`.

# CLI reference · ultrafast docs

> Every ultrafast command: new, check, sheet, render, review, inspect, live, export, serve, mcp and more. The CLI is ultrafast, or uf for short.

# The CLI

`ultrafast`, or `uf` for short. Every command answers in JSON or in files you can look at.

## Start

  * [Quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)
  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

  * [Render video from JSON](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/render-video-from-json/>)
  * [Personalized videos from a CSV](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/>)
  * [Make a video with Claude Code](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/claude-code/>)
  * [Lottie to MP4, WebM or ProRes](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/lottie-to-mp4/>)

  * [Ops](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/>)
  * [CLI](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>)
  * [MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>)
  * [HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>)

## For agents

  * [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>)

**On this page**

  1. Make
  2. Export
