# Render benchmark: ultrafast vs Remotion vs HyperFrames · ultrafast

> Render benchmark on one RTX 5090: 10-second videos in 0.66–0.78 s with ultrafast; Remotion 2.25–6.69 s and HyperFrames 3.31–4.46 s at their fastest settings.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/

# ultrafast, Remotion and HyperFrames, timed.

Three 10-second videos, exported on one RTX 5090 workstation. ultrafast took 0.66 to 0.78 s. Remotion took 2.25 to 6.69 s and HyperFrames 3.31 to 4.46 s, each at the fastest setting found.

Measured 22 November 2026, and ultrafast 0.2.0 again on the night of 23 November 2026. ultrafast ran the benchmark and wrote this page. The code, every run and the frames are in the [benchmark repository](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>), with one script to reproduce it.

## Faster in every scene and every setting.

Seconds from the start of each tool's render command to the finished MP4. Median of 5 warm runs, 300 frames each. At the fastest setting found, Remotion took 3.1 to 8.6 times as long as ultrafast, and HyperFrames 4.6 to 5.7 times. With their default commands: 6.2 to 10.9 times, and 5.2 to 6.5 times.

### Title card 1080×1920, 10 s, fastest setting found

  1. ultrafast **0.66 s**
  2. Remotion **2.32 s**
  3. HyperFrames **3.53 s**

### Chart 1920×1080, 10 s, fastest setting found

  1. ultrafast **0.72 s**
  2. Remotion **2.25 s**
  3. HyperFrames **3.31 s**

### Footage 1080×1920, 10 s, fastest setting found

  1. ultrafast **0.78 s**
  2. Remotion **6.69 s**
  3. HyperFrames **4.46 s**

Scene| ultrafast| Remotion, fastest found| Remotion, default| HyperFrames, fastest found| HyperFrames, default  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
Title card| **0.66**|  2.32 (3.5×)| 4.73 (7.2×)| 3.53 (5.3×)| 3.92 (5.9×)  
Chart| **0.72**|  2.25 (3.1×)| 4.45 (6.2×)| 3.31 (4.6×)| 3.71 (5.2×)  
Footage| **0.78**|  6.69 (8.6×)| 8.53 (10.9×)| 4.46 (5.7×)| 5.05 (6.5×)  
  
Seconds, lower is better. In brackets: that time divided by ultrafast's. “Fastest found” is the quickest of every configuration measured for that tool on that scene (how it was searched). On the title card and the footage, Remotion's fastest run used NVENC at its default quality, which is lower than the CRF 18 used everywhere else. A fourth scene, effects, is reported apart.

## The first run, and one frame.

A cold first run took 1.8 to 2.1 s with ultrafast, 8.4 to 12.6 s with Remotion and 3.7 to 5.6 s with HyperFrames. One still frame took 0.20 to 0.70 s, against 2.2 to 2.3 s and 1.5 to 2.1 s.

Cold first run, default command, seconds Scene| ultrafast| Remotion| HyperFrames  
---|---|---|---  
Title card| 1.77| 8.46| 3.93  
Chart| 2.09| 8.41| 3.66  
Footage| 1.99| 12.56| 5.55  
  
The first render after deleting each tool's own caches. ultrafast compiles its GPU pipelines, Remotion runs webpack without its cache, and HyperFrames extracts the video frames again. The operating system's file cache is kept, so this is not a cold boot.

One still frame at 5 s, warm median, seconds Scene| ultrafast| Remotion| HyperFrames  
---|---|---|---  
Title card| 0.22| 2.19| 1.52  
Chart| 0.20| 2.16| 1.52  
Footage| 0.70| 2.29| 2.10  
  
One PNG of frame 150 from each CLI: `ultrafast render --at 5`, `remotion still --frame=150`, `hyperframes snapshot --at 5`. It stands in for the time to a first preview frame.

## Fewer tokens to write it.

A separate count. The same 10-second vertical short was written for each tool the way its docs and agent skills teach: NASA footage, an animated title, three lines of detail, captions timed to each word, a grade and grain. Tokens counted with tiktoken `o200k_base`.

  1. ultrafast **1,234**
  2. Remotion **1,868**
  3. HyperFrames **1,680**
  4. Shotstack **1,657**

| Files written, whole| Typed after the scaffold| What the agent writes  
---|---|---|---  
ultrafast 0.1.1| **1,234**| **1,218**|  one JSON document  
Remotion 4.0.545| 1,868| 1,660| a React and TypeScript composition, a config line and two CLI commands  
HyperFrames 0.9.79| 1,680| 1,500| one HTML file (CSS and a GSAP timeline) and one CLI command  
Shotstack| 1,657| 1,657| an Edit JSON and an SRT file; written and validated, not rendered  
  
Counting only what is typed after each tool's own scaffold step, the ultrafast document is 19% fewer tokens than HyperFrames, and 27% fewer than Remotion and Shotstack.

The tokenizer is OpenAI's `o200k_base`, not Claude's: the ratios should roughly hold, and the absolute counts will differ. Counts depend on authoring style; each version is one competent way to write it, not a minimum. Shotstack's version was never rendered, because that needs an account, so whether its frames match is unknown; Shotstack is not in the render benchmark. Lockfiles, `node_modules`, untouched scaffold files, render commands and code the tools generate are not counted. Per-file counts and the method: [tokens/RESULTS.md](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks/blob/main/tokens/RESULTS.md>).

## How it was measured.

Each tool ran its own render command on the same workstation, with the clock running from launch until the MP4 was on disk.

### The machine

One workstation: an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 (16 cores, 32 threads), an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and Fedora Linux 45. ultrafast 0.2.0 (the release binary, on Vulkan), Remotion 4.0.545 and HyperFrames 0.9.79, each with the Chrome headless shell it pins.

### The videos

  * **Title card** , 1080×1920: a gradient, shapes, staggered type, a fade and a slide out.
  * **Chart** , 1920×1080: 12 bars growing with counters and labels, a target line drawing on, a legend.
  * **Footage** , 1080×1920: a NASA clip of Orion approaching the Moon, a push-in, a shade and word-timed karaoke captions.

Each is 10 s at 30 fps, so every render is 300 frames, written to an H.264 MP4 with `--crf 18` in all three tools. Each scene is written the way the tool's docs teach, with the same font files and the same clip.

### The clock

The number is the wall-clock time of the tool's own render command. It covers everything a user waits for: process start, bundling (Remotion), browser launch (Remotion and HyperFrames), GPU start-up and shader compilation (ultrafast), rendering, encoding and muxing. Warm is the median of 5 runs after one warm-up run. Cold is the first run after deleting the tool's own caches.

### A quiet machine

Before every run, the harness waited until no other renderer was working, other processes used at most 1.5 of the 32 CPU threads, and the GPU was under 15% busy. If other load showed up during a run, that run was thrown out and repeated. 560 runs counted, and none failed. ultrafast's rows were measured again with the 0.2.0 release on the night of 23 November 2026, the same way; Remotion and HyperFrames were not re-run. Three of those ultrafast runs were thrown out for other load and repeated, and one cold run was set aside and measured again because it had not started cold. As a control, 0.1.1 ran 3 to 5% slower that night than the night before, so the second night did not favour ultrafast.

Every output was checked with ffprobe: H.264, the right size, exactly 300 decoded frames, 10.0 s, 30 fps. A run counted only if its output passed.

### How “fastest found” was searched

ultrafast ran its default command only; its `export --workers` option was left at its default. Remotion and HyperFrames got their default command, and then:

  * **A concurrency sweep.** Remotion at 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 32 browser tabs; HyperFrames at 2, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 24 workers; twice each. Both tools' docs say to find this setting by benchmarking.
  * **The maximum.** `--concurrency 32` for Remotion and `--workers 24` for HyperFrames.
  * **A prebuilt bundle.** Remotion rendering from `npx remotion bundle` made beforehand, so the timed command has no webpack step.
  * **GPU flags.** Remotion with `--gl=angle-egl`, the option its docs give for Linux, and with `--gl=vulkan`, swept again at 8 to 32 tabs from the prebuilt bundle. On this machine `angle-egl` ran on the integrated Radeon GPU; `vulkan` used the RTX 5090.
  * **NVENC.** Remotion with `--hardware-acceleration if-possible`, which Remotion allows only without `--crf`, so at NVENC's default quality. HyperFrames with `--gpu`, alone and with the sweep's worker count.

The headline compares ultrafast with each tool's default command (Remotion's uses 8 tabs here; HyperFrames' `--workers auto` chose 6) and with the fastest of all its configurations:

Scene| Remotion, fastest found| HyperFrames, fastest found  
---|---|---  
Title card| prebuilt bundle, `--gl=vulkan`, NVENC, `--concurrency 24`| `--workers 8`  
Chart| prebuilt bundle, `--gl=angle-egl`, `--concurrency 16`| `--workers 4`  
Footage| prebuilt bundle, `--gl=vulkan`, NVENC, `--concurrency 8`| `--workers 8`  
  
Every configuration with its timings, CPU, memory, GPU use and file size is in [the repository's README](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks#every-measured-configuration>).

## The same picture from all three.

The same six moments from each tool's video, one row per tool: ultrafast, then Remotion, then HyperFrames. Over all 300 frames, luma SSIM against ultrafast's video is 0.985 to 0.993 on the title card and chart, and 0.936 to 0.948 on the footage.

![Title card frames at 0.5, 1.5, 3, 5, 7 and 9.5 seconds from ultrafast, Remotion and HyperFrames, one row each. A yellow circle, a cyan shape and the words Make it move on a purple-to-pink gradient look the same in all three rows.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/bench/title.webp) Title card, 1080×1920. ![Footage frames at the same six moments from the three tools: NASA footage of the Moon with word-timed captions, one word highlighted in yellow. The rows match.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/bench/footage.webp) Footage, 1080×1920, NASA.

![Chart frames at the same six moments from the three tools: twelve blue bars growing to a pink final bar, with a target line and legend. The rows match.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/bench/chart.webp) Chart, 1920×1080. Contact sheets of all 10 frames per tool are in [frames/](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks/tree/main/frames>).

## The effects scene, reported apart.

A fourth scene, 1920×1080: blurred colour fields, a glowing title, a motion-blurred whip, grain and a vignette. It is not like-for-like, so it is not in the headline.

Blur, glow, motion blur and grain are cheap on a GPU and slow in Chrome. The three looks are also close, not identical: the grain is random noise drawn differently in each, and the blurs are computed differently. The scene shows the size of that effect, nothing more.

Warm median: ultrafast 0.74 s. Remotion 2.98 s at its fastest setting found, 5.95 s with its default command. HyperFrames 5.23 s at its fastest, 6.42 s by default.

![Effects frames at six moments from ultrafast, Remotion and HyperFrames: blurred purple, cyan and red fields behind a glowing GLOW title. The blur and the background differ between the rows.](https://ultrafast.mov/img/bench/effects.webp) Effects, 1920×1080: ultrafast, Remotion, HyperFrames. The looks differ.

## Where ultrafast does worse.

Read these before quoting a number.

### Larger files than Remotion's

At the same nominal `--crf 18`, ultrafast's NVENC files for the title card, chart and footage are 1.15 to 1.75 times the size of Remotion's libx264 files, and 0.62 to 1.23 times HyperFrames'. The title card is 1.1 MB, against 0.6 MB and 1.1 MB. On the effects scene they are about a tenth of the size.

### It needs a GPU

A Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU. Without one, the Docker image renders on the CPU through Mesa's software Vulkan driver, which is much slower. Remotion and HyperFrames need no GPU.

### No prebuilt Windows or Intel Mac build

Releases are for Macs with Apple silicon and for Linux x86_64. On Windows with an NVIDIA GPU, ultrafast is built from source through WSL2. Remotion and HyperFrames run wherever Node and Chrome do.

### One machine

Every number comes from one workstation with a large GPU: Remotion and HyperFrames on 22 November 2026, ultrafast 0.2.0 on the night of 23 November 2026. That is a GPU engine against browser engines on hardware that suits the GPU engine. On a machine without a capable GPU the comparison is different.

### Other caveats

  * **The encoders differ.** ultrafast 0.2.0 reads `--crf` on libx264's scale: CRF 18 becomes NVENC's constant quality 24, which matched libx264's CRF 18 picture within 0.3 VMAF points on these scenes. Close, not identical. Swapping in NVENC barely moved the browser tools: HyperFrames with `--gpu` was 0.1 to 0.4 s slower than with libx264 at the same worker count, and Remotion with NVENC ranged from 0.22 s faster to 0.04 s slower.
  * **Most of ultrafast's time is start-up.** Of 0.66 to 0.78 s per render, its own log gives 0.22 to 0.36 s for rendering and encoding the 300 frames. The rest is process and GPU start-up and muxing. Only 10-second videos were measured.
  * **Video decoding differs.** Remotion decodes the clip in every browser tab, so more tabs made it slower on the footage: 8.6 s at 8 tabs, 21.7 s at 32. HyperFrames extracts the frames once and reuses them on warm runs.
  * **“Cold” is not a cold boot.** ultrafast's cold run compiles its GPU pipelines, which adds about 1.1 to 1.4 s. The operating system's file cache is not dropped, and the browsers stay installed.
  * **Idiomatic, not hand-tuned.** Each scene is written the way the tool's docs teach. Someone who knows a tool well could probably make it faster. The source for all three is in the repository.

## Run it yourself.

You need Linux with cgroup v2 and systemd, an NVIDIA GPU with `nvidia-smi`, Node 22 or newer, Python 3, FFmpeg and ffprobe, and the ultrafast 0.2.0 release. A full run takes one to two hours.

```
git clone https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks
cd benchmarks
./setup.sh                               # the pinned npm packages, browsers and FFmpeg, in this folder
UF=/path/to/ultrafast ./run.sh --fresh   # the render benchmark; or put ultrafast 0.2.0 on PATH
pip install tiktoken && python3 tokens/tokens.py   # the token count
``` 

Nothing in it is random: the scenes are pure functions of time, and the runs go in a fixed order. `run.sh` writes `results.json`, `results/tables.md` and `frames/`. Product names belong to their owners.

## Make one and time it.

Install the engine and time a render on your own GPU.

`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` [Read the quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)

Want it hosted? [Join the ultrafast Cloud waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).

# Open source Remotion alternatives, compared · ultrafast

> Remotion alternatives that are open source: Revideo, Motion Canvas, HyperFrames, Framefields, VideoFlow, Editly, Manim and ultrafast, and when to pick each.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/remotion/

# Open-source Remotion alternatives.

Eight tools that make video from code under an open-source licence, and when each one fits better than Remotion.

Updated 22 November 2026. ultrafast wrote this page and is one of the eight. Every figure is from each project's own repository and docs; sources are at the end.

## Why people look elsewhere.

Three reasons come up, each in Remotion's own words. Its pages were read on 22 November 2026.

### A company licence from 4 people

The free licence is “for individuals and companies of up to 3 people.” The terms count everyone: “Headcount means all personnel, regardless of whether they use the Remotion Software.” So a company of 4 needs a company licence even if one person makes the videos.

[Pricing](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/license/pricing>) · [Terms](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/terms#TeamSize>)

### A fee for every render

The licence for automated rendering is “$0.01 per render, charged in increments of 1000 renders ($10), with a minimum of $100 per month.” The per-seat licence is “$25 per month per seat.” On Lambda, “Teams of 4+ people also need to acquire a Remotion Company License in addition to the AWS cost.”

[Pricing](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/license/pricing>) · [Lambda cost example](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/lambda/cost-example>)

### Chrome draws every frame

“Remotion downloads ‘Chrome Headless Shell’ into your `node_modules` to render videos.” Locally, “each Chrome tab renders web content and then screenshots it.” And: “By default in many cases, the GPU is disabled in headless mode, which can lead to a significant slowdown in rendering time.”

[Chrome Headless Shell](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/miscellaneous/chrome-headless-shell>) · [Concurrency](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/terminology/concurrency>) · [GPU](<https://www.remotion.dev/docs/gpu>)

Remotion's source is public under its own Remotion License. Its two tiers were “designed to ensure funding for this project while still allowing the source code to be available and the program to be free for most.” The tools below use open-source licences, MIT or Apache-2.0, so they are free for a company of any size. A few sell extras, noted below.

## Eight alternatives, side by side.

In alphabetical order, with Remotion first for reference. Stars, licences and dates from the GitHub API, checked 22 November 2026.

Project| Licence| You write| How it renders| Agent tooling| GPU| Latest release · last commit| Stars  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
[Remotion](<https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion>) for reference| Remotion License, source-available; a company licence from 4 people| React and TypeScript| Chrome Headless Shell; each tab renders the page and screenshots it; FFmpeg encodes| 13 Agent Skills; plugins for 5 coding agents; its hosted MCP server shut down on 26 October 2026| often off in headless Chrome; none on Lambda| v4.0.545, 18 Nov 2026 · 20 Nov 2026| 74,759  
[Editly](<https://github.com/mifi/editly>)| MIT| a JSON5 edit spec, or JavaScript| Node.js and FFmpeg, streaming; Canvas and Fabric.js layers; GL transitions| none found| GL shaders through headless-gl; no GPU in its requirements| v0.15.0-rc.1, 19 Jan 2025 (npm: 0.14.2, Dec 2022) · 20 Feb 2025| 5,638  
[Framefields](<https://github.com/gatewai-dev/framefields>)| Apache-2.0| TypeScript| WebGPU in Node through Dawn (Metal, Vulkan, D3D12); no browser; hardware-encoded MP4| 7 skills and a Claude Code plugin; agents inspect frame grids| renders on it; a CPU fallback (lavapipe or WARP) is about 10 to 12 times slower| npm 3.0.2, 13 Nov 2026 · 18 Nov 2026| 529  
[HyperFrames](<https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes>) by HeyGen| Apache-2.0| HTML, CSS and JavaScript with a seekable animation (GSAP or another adapter)| headless Chrome through Puppeteer seeks and captures each frame; 1 to 24 workers; FFmpeg encodes| 9 skills; plugins for 6 agents; a hosted MCP server that renders on HeyGen| optional: `--browser-gpu` for capture, `--gpu` for hardware encoding| v0.9.79, 21 Nov 2026 · 21 Nov 2026| 87,831  
[Manim](<https://github.com/ManimCommunity/manim>) Community edition| MIT| Python| Cairo by default, or OpenGL; PyAV (FFmpeg's libraries) writes the video| none found| with the optional OpenGL renderer| v0.22.1, 27 Oct 2026 · 21 Nov 2026| 42,775 3b1b/manim: 96,778  
[Motion Canvas](<https://github.com/motion-canvas/motion-canvas>)| MIT| TypeScript, with generators| its editor draws each frame on a canvas in your browser; an image sequence, or video through the FFmpeg exporter| none found| no GPU in its requirements| v3.17.2, 14 Dec 2024 · 2 Jul 2026| 20,124  
[Revideo](<https://github.com/midrender/revideo>)| MIT| TypeScript scenes as generator functions| headless Chrome through Puppeteer draws each frame on a canvas; WebCodecs encodes; FFmpeg adds the audio; parallel workers| none found| none required: it runs where Node and a headless browser run| v0.11.0, 10 Jul 2026 · 15 Jul 2026| 4,223  
[ultrafast](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast>)| Apache-2.0 or MIT| one JSON document, checked before it renders| GPU kernels on Metal or Vulkan; H.264 and HEVC encoded on the same GPU; no browser| 20 MCP tools, a skill and a Claude Code plugin; `check`, `review` and `inspect`| renders on it; needs an Apple silicon Mac or Linux with a Vulkan GPU| v0.2.0, 23 Nov 2026 · 23 Nov 2026| 0  
[VideoFlow](<https://github.com/ybouane/VideoFlow>)| Apache-2.0 (its React editor has its own licence)| TypeScript, compiled to a portable JSON format| headless Chromium on a server, or WebCodecs in the browser; WebGL effects| llms.txt and Markdown docs| no GPU in its requirements| 1.3.4, 16 Sep 2026 · 16 Sep 2026| 174  
  
“None found”: no skills, MCP server or agent plugin in the repository or docs. Dates are UTC. A release is the latest GitHub release, or the latest npm version where the project publishes there. The last commit is on the default branch. Product names belong to their owners.

## Which one to choose.

Each tool is the better fit for some jobs. Remotion included.

### Choose Remotion when

  * Your team builds in React and wants to reuse its components.
  * You need an embeddable web player.
  * You want a project in development since 2020, with 74,759 stars, and the licence fits: 3 people or fewer, or a company licence.

### Choose Editly when

  * You are cutting clips, photos, titles and music together from a JSON5 file or the command line.
  * You want an MIT tool that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with Node and FFmpeg.
  * You don't need recent updates: the last commit was in February 2025.

### Choose Framefields when

  * You want to write TypeScript and render on the GPU with no browser.
  * You need Windows (D3D12), or a CPU fallback for CI.
  * You want PBR materials and glTF models, or on-device vision such as SAM tracking.
  * You can work with beta software. Its AI gateway for generated media and its cloud GPU renders are optional and paid.

### Choose HyperFrames when

  * Your team writes HTML, CSS and GSAP.
  * You want a large, fast-moving project: 87,831 stars and a release on 21 November 2026.
  * You are porting Remotion code: it ships a `/remotion-to-hyperframes` skill.
  * You need HDR or HLS output, or hosted renders on HeyGen, which its MCP server uses.

### Choose Manim when

  * You are animating maths in Python: equations, graphs and geometry.
  * You want the edition its maintainers recommend for new work, the Community edition; or Grant Sanderson's original, 3b1b/manim (96,778 stars), to study how the 3Blue1Brown videos are made.

### Choose Motion Canvas when

  * You make vector explainers timed to a voice-over, in a real-time editor.
  * You render from the editor, don't need a server or an API, and don't mind that the last release was in December 2024.

### Choose Revideo when

  * You want generator-based TypeScript scenes rendered from code or an endpoint, with a React player for previews.
  * You want to split renders across workers on serverless machines.
  * You accept anonymous render counts, or set `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true` to turn them off.

### Choose VideoFlow when

  * You want one JSON format to render on a server, in the browser, or as live playback with scrubbing.
  * You build a web app around video. Its core and renderers are Apache-2.0; its React Video Editor needs a company licence beyond 3 employees.

### Choose ultrafast when

  * An agent writes the video and should check and review its own frames before you watch.
  * You want 3D, particles, fluid and shaders in the same video as the type and the footage.
  * You render often on your own GPU and want no per-render fee at any company size.

## Shot on the GPU.

Shaders, 3D, motion type and camera optics, written by your agent and rendered on the GPU. Open source.

Apache-2.0 or MIT, for everyone. No per-render fee and no licence tiers, at any company size.

ultrafast, measured on one RTX 5090

1080p, 6-sample motion blur
    894 fps
10 s hero, 300 frames
    0.34 s
launch film, 16 s, 3D
    4.88 s
simulation, 15 s
    1.06 s
vertical teaser, 10 s, 3D
    1.68 s

Export times for every film are on [examples](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/>). No other tool on this page has been timed on the same machine, so this page compares no speeds.

Measured on one RTX 5090 workstation, end to end: three 10-second videos (a title card, an animated chart and captioned NASA footage) exported in 0.66 to 0.78 s with ultrafast, against 2.25 to 6.69 s for Remotion and 3.31 to 4.46 s for HyperFrames at the fastest setting found for each. Only these three tools were measured. [Method and raw results](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>).

### Agents see their frames

`check` finds mistakes before rendering. Frames and contact sheets come back as images. `review` reads every frame for unreadable, clipped, overlapping or too-brief text and flashing. `inspect` names the node behind a pixel.

### One graph for all of it

3D with image-based light, raymarching, particles, fluid and feedback simulations, and Slang shaders, in the same document as the type and the footage.

### Built for agents

20 MCP tools over stdio with `uf mcp`, or 16 over HTTP from your own `uf serve`. A skill, and a Claude Code plugin with both. See the [MCP docs](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>).

### Where ultrafast doesn't fit

  * No React. A video is a JSON document, not components.
  * No embeddable web player. The live player is a desktop window; for the web, export an MP4.
  * It needs a GPU: a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU.
  * No prebuilt Windows or Intel Mac build yet.
  * No hosted rendering yet. ultrafast Cloud has a [waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).
  * It is new: the first release came out on 21 November 2026.

## Moving from Remotion.

ultrafast doesn't run React, so a Remotion project is rebuilt, not imported. There are two ways to start.

### Ask your coding agent

Give it the composition and ask for the same video in ultrafast. With the ultrafast skill installed, the agent knows the document format and the loop: check, look at the frames, review, export. The skill works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI.

### Reconstruct a render

`uf reconstruct` turns a finished video into an editable draft: shots, text layers in matched fonts, backgrounds and fades, with a report of each decision. It reads text with Apple Vision on macOS, or with Tesseract (installed separately) elsewhere. A shot it can't explain as a gradient or a still keeps the video itself as its background.

```
npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast                       # the skill, for your coding agent
uf reconstruct render.mp4 --out-dir rec                     # writes rec/reconstruction.json
uf check rec/reconstruction.json && uf sheet rec/reconstruction.json --out rec/sheet.png
``` 

More in the [CLI reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>) and [RECONSTRUCTION.md](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/blob/main/docs/RECONSTRUCTION.md>).

# HyperFrames alternatives, compared · ultrafast

> Alternatives to HyperFrames for video from code: Remotion, Revideo, Motion Canvas, Framefields, VideoFlow, Editly, Manim and ultrafast, which renders on the GPU with no browser.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/hyperframes/

# HyperFrames alternatives.

HyperFrames turns HTML into video in headless Chrome. Eight tools that make video from code another way, and when each one fits better.

Updated 23 November 2026. ultrafast wrote this page and is one of the eight. Every figure is from each project's own repository and docs; sources are at the end.

## Why people look elsewhere.

HyperFrames is open source (Apache-2.0) and moves fast: 88,793 stars and a release on 23 November 2026. The reasons to look elsewhere are about the renderer, in HyperFrames' own words.

### A browser draws every frame

“Rendering never plays your video. It asks for one frame at a time.” Each frame is seeked, then “Chrome's `HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame` grabs the pixels,” and “FFmpeg turns the captured frames into the MP4.” Parallel renders use 1 to 24 workers: “Each is a separate Chrome, roughly 256 MB.”

[Deterministic rendering](<https://hyperframes.heygen.com/concepts/determinism>) · [CLI](<https://hyperframes.heygen.com/packages/cli>)

### Render time is page work

Its performance guide times one composition built two ways: “25.0s against 9.8s, taken as the median of three runs at 1920x1080 over 300 frames. One CSS declaration is the whole difference.” Its advice is to “use fewer large `backdrop-filter` and `filter: blur()` layers.”

[Fix a slow preview or render](<https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/performance>)

### Pixels can move between machines

“Fonts and Chrome versions differ between computers, so a local render can shift by a pixel from one machine to the next. Render in Docker when you need exact reproducibility.”

[Deterministic rendering](<https://hyperframes.heygen.com/concepts/determinism>)

None of this makes HyperFrames a poor choice. A web page is a good way to lay out type, and the browser's cost is the price of using it. The tools below either draw with something other than a browser, or ask you to describe the video another way.

## Eight alternatives, side by side.

In alphabetical order, with HyperFrames first for reference. Stars, licences and dates from the GitHub API, checked 23 November 2026.

---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---

[Editly](<https://github.com/mifi/editly>)| MIT| a JSON5 edit spec, or JavaScript| Node.js and FFmpeg, streaming; Canvas and Fabric.js layers; GL transitions| none found| GL shaders through headless-gl; no GPU in its requirements| v0.15.0-rc.1, 19 Jan 2025 (npm: 0.14.2, Dec 2022) · 20 Feb 2025| 5,647

## Which one to choose.

Each tool is the better fit for some jobs. HyperFrames included.

### Stay with HyperFrames when

  * Your team writes HTML, CSS and GSAP, or has compositions in them already.
  * You want HeyGen's avatars and voices, its Studio app, or hosted renders on HeyGen.
  * You need HDR or HLS output today.

### Choose Editly when

  * You are cutting clips, photos, titles and music together from a JSON5 file or the command line.
  * You want an MIT tool that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with Node and FFmpeg.
  * You don't need recent updates: the last commit was in February 2025.

### Choose Framefields when

  * You want to keep writing TypeScript but render on the GPU with no browser.
  * You need Windows (D3D12), or a CPU fallback for CI.
  * You can work with beta software. Its AI gateway for generated media and its cloud GPU renders are optional and paid.

### Choose Manim when

  * You are animating maths in Python: equations, graphs and geometry.
  * You want a large, long-lived community: 42,850 stars on the Community edition.

### Choose Motion Canvas when

  * You make vector explainers timed to a voice-over, in a real-time editor.
  * You render from the editor, don't need a server or an API, and don't mind that the last release was in December 2024.

### Choose Remotion when

  * Your team builds in React and wants to reuse its components.
  * You need an embeddable web player.
  * The licence fits: 3 people or fewer, or a company licence. It still renders in Chrome.

### Choose Revideo when

  * You want generator-based TypeScript scenes rendered from code or an endpoint, with a React player for previews.
  * You want to split renders across workers on serverless machines. It also renders in headless Chrome.

### Choose VideoFlow when

  * You want one JSON format to render on a server, in the browser, or as live playback with scrubbing.
  * You build a web app around video. Its core and renderers are Apache-2.0; its React Video Editor needs a company licence beyond 3 employees.

### Choose ultrafast when

  * You want no browser in the render: the frame is drawn and encoded on the GPU.
  * An agent writes the video and should check and review its own frames before you watch.
  * You want 3D, particles, fluid and shaders in the same video as the type and the footage, without a page doing the work.
  * You need the same pixels on every machine without pinning a browser.

## Shot on the GPU.

Shaders, 3D, motion type and camera optics, written by your agent and rendered on the GPU. Open source, Apache-2.0 or MIT.

Measured on one RTX 5090 workstation, end to end: three 10-second videos (a title card, an animated chart and captioned NASA footage) exported in 0.66 to 0.78 s with ultrafast. At the fastest setting found for each, HyperFrames took 4.6 to 5.7 times as long, and Remotion 3.1 to 8.6 times. No other tool on this page was measured. [Method and results](<https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/>).

### Agents see their frames

`check` finds mistakes before rendering. Frames and contact sheets come back as images. `review` reads every frame for unreadable, clipped, overlapping or too-brief text and flashing. `inspect` names the node behind a pixel.

### Built for agents

20 MCP tools over stdio with `uf mcp`, or 16 over HTTP from your own `uf serve`. A skill, and a Claude Code plugin with both. See the [video MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/mcp/>).

### Where ultrafast doesn't fit

  * No HTML or CSS. A video is a JSON document, not a web page.
  * No embeddable web player. The live player is a desktop window; for the web, export an MP4.
  * It is built for a GPU: a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU. Without one, the Docker image renders on the CPU, much more slowly.
  * No prebuilt Windows or Intel Mac build yet, and no HDR or HLS output.
  * No hosted rendering yet. ultrafast Cloud has a [waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).
  * It is new: the first release came out on 21 November 2026.

## Moving from HyperFrames.

ultrafast doesn't run HTML, so a HyperFrames composition is rebuilt, not imported. There are two ways to start.

### Ask your coding agent

Give it the composition and ask for the same video in ultrafast. With the ultrafast skill installed, the agent knows the document format and the loop: check, look at the frames, review, export. The skill works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI.

### Reconstruct a render

`uf reconstruct` turns a finished video into an editable draft: shots, text layers in matched fonts, backgrounds and fades, with a report of each decision. A shot it can't explain as a gradient or a still keeps the video itself as its background.

```
npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast                       # the skill, for your coding agent
uf reconstruct render.mp4 --out-dir rec                     # writes rec/reconstruction.json
uf check rec/reconstruction.json && uf sheet rec/reconstruction.json --out rec/sheet.png
``` 

More in the [CLI reference](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>), the head-to-head on [ultrafast vs HyperFrames](<https://ultrafast.mov/compare/hyperframes/>), and the [Remotion alternatives](<https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/remotion/>).

## Common questions.

Is HyperFrames open source?

Yes. HyperFrames is Apache-2.0, from HeyGen. So are Framefields and VideoFlow's core; Editly, Manim, Motion Canvas and Revideo are MIT; ultrafast is Apache-2.0 or MIT. Remotion is source-available under its own licence, with a company licence from 4 people.

Which HyperFrames alternatives don't use a browser?

ultrafast (GPU kernels on Metal or Vulkan), Framefields (WebGPU in Node through Dawn), Manim (Cairo or OpenGL) and Editly (Node.js, Canvas and FFmpeg). Remotion, Revideo and VideoFlow's server renderer use headless Chrome, and Motion Canvas renders from its editor in your browser.

Which one is fastest?

Only three tools have been timed on the same machine: on one RTX 5090, three 10-second videos exported in 0.66 to 0.78 s with ultrafast, and HyperFrames took 4.6 to 5.7 times as long at its fastest setting found. The method and raw results are in the [benchmark](<https://ultrafast.mov/benchmarks/>). The other tools on this page weren't measured.

Can I bring my HyperFrames compositions to ultrafast?

Not as files: ultrafast doesn't run HTML. Ask your coding agent to rewrite the composition as an ultrafast document (the ultrafast skill teaches it the format), or run `uf reconstruct` on a finished render to get an editable draft.

Do I need a GPU?

For ultrafast and Framefields, a GPU is the fast path. ultrafast runs on a Mac with Apple silicon or Linux with a Vulkan GPU; its Docker image also renders on the CPU, much more slowly. HyperFrames, Remotion, Revideo and VideoFlow run on CPUs, with Chrome doing the drawing.

# Open-source alternative to Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate · ultrafast

> Render JSON to video on your own GPU instead of a per-minute API: ultrafast compared with Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate on price, formats, 3D, self-hosting and agent tools.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/alternatives/json-to-video-api/

# JSON to video, on your own GPU.

Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate render your JSON in their cloud and charge by the minute. ultrafast is an open-source engine that renders it on your own GPU. Here is what each one does better, from their own docs.

Updated 23 November 2026. ultrafast wrote this page. Every vendor figure is from that vendor's own pages; sources are at the end. Prices marked “about” are worked out from the vendor's published credit rules.

## Four ways to render a JSON video.

The three APIs are hosted services. ultrafast is a binary, a Docker image and an HTTP server you run yourself.

| ultrafast| Shotstack| JSON2Video| Creatomate  
---|---|---|---|---  
Where it renders| your GPU: a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux with a Vulkan GPU; much more slowly on the CPU in Docker| Shotstack's cloud; the Studio SDK can also export in the browser| JSON2Video's cloud| Creatomate's cloud  
Self-hosted| `uf serve`: an HTTP API and a remote MCP server on one machine| not offered| not offered| not offered  
Licence| Apache-2.0 or MIT, engine included| proprietary service; Studio SDK under PolyForm Shield (source-available); CLI Apache-2.0| proprietary service; CLI and SDKs MIT| proprietary service; Preview SDK and libraries MIT  
Price per rendered minute| no fee; your GPU's time| 5¢ to 20¢, by plan; 4K from the $99 Pro plan| one credit per second: about 17¢ to 42¢| credits by pixels × frames: about 84¢ for 1080p at 30 fps on Essential, billed yearly  
Free to start| free for any use, commercial included| 10 credits on sign-up, valid 30 days; watermarked sandbox| 600 credits once; watermarked, up to 60 s, no commercial use| 50 credits; renders are previews of up to 480 px  
The JSON| a graph of nodes with animated params and timing windows, checked against a [published schema](<https://ultrafast.mov/schema/v1.json>)| an Edit: a timeline of tracks and clips, 16 asset types, merge fields| a Movie: scenes played back to back, 9 element types, variables| RenderScript: 6 element types, keyframes, nested compositions  
3D and shaders| 3D (glTF, extruded type, image-based light, glass), Slang shaders, particles, fluid| not documented| not documented| 3D-style transforms only  
Lottie| as editable vector nodes ([guide](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/lottie-to-mp4/>))| inside the `html5` asset, captured from a browser page, which Shotstack calls “the heaviest to render”| not documented| not documented  
Output| H.264, HEVC and AV1 MP4; ProRes up to 4444 XQ; transparent ProRes and WebM; GIF; PNG and EXR sequences; sound alone| mp4, gif, mp3, jpg, png, bmp| MP4, and an MP3 audio track on paid plans| mp4, jpg, png, gif  
Frame rate| any| 12 to 60 fps| “Currently every movie renders at 25 fps”| at most 60 fps  
Largest size| any size; presets up to 4K on the short side| 3840 px a side| 3840 px a side, by plan| 3840 px a side  
For agents| 20 MCP tools locally, 16 over HTTP; `check` before rendering, `review` of every frame after| hosted MCP with OAuth; a CLI and skill that validate edits offline| hosted and local MCP, 15 tools including `validate_movie`| hosted MCP with OAuth  
Output tokens for a 10 s short| about 1,234, measured| about 1,657, measured (validated, not rendered)| not measured| not measured  
No-code| none; call the HTTP API| not checked for this page| Make, n8n, Zapier| Zapier, Make, n8n and about 30 more  
Templates and editors| five starter documents (`uf new`); no visual editor| Studio editor and a templates API| visual editor and “dozens” of templates| template editor; embeddable Preview SDK  
Voices and transcripts| captions from Whisper, SRT or VTT you bring; voiceover with macOS voices or eSpeak NG| transcription in 99 languages; text to speech| ElevenLabs and Azure voices; automatic subtitles| automatic subtitles  
  
Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate are trademarks of their owners. Token counts are from the [benchmark repository](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>) (tiktoken o200k_base, the same 10-second short written for each tool). None of the three hosted services can be timed on the same machine as ultrafast, so this page compares no render speeds.

## Which one to choose.

A hosted API is the right call for many teams. Here is where each side wins.

### Choose a hosted API when

  * You have no GPU and don't want to run a server. All three take a request and send back a link.
  * You need many renders at once, webhooks or delivery to your own storage. `uf serve` renders one job at a time on one GPU.
  * Your workflow lives in Zapier, Make or n8n, or non-developers edit templates in a visual editor.
  * You want transcription, stock voices or generated media inside the same API.
  * You want a Claude or ChatGPT connector with OAuth today. ultrafast's comes with [ultrafast Cloud](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>), which has a waitlist.

### Choose ultrafast when

  * You render a lot and the per-minute bill matters, or the footage can't leave your machine. Inputs are local files.
  * You need ProRes, HEVC, AV1, transparent video or a frame rate other than 25, 30 or 60.
  * The video needs 3D, shaders, particles or real motion blur, not only clips, text and transitions.
  * An agent writes the JSON and should check it before rendering and review every frame after.
  * You want the engine's source under a licence that lets you ship it.

## Run the API yourself.

One container on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU. It prints its API key on first start.

```
docker run --gpus all -p 8080:8080 -v ultrafast:/data \
  ghcr.io/ultrafastmov/ultrafast:latest serve

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/render \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ULTRAFAST_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"document": '"$(cat video.json)"', "output": {"codec": "h264", "size": "1080p"}}' \
  -o video.mp4
``` 

The same server answers MCP at `/mcp`, and has endpoints to check a document, render a single frame or a contact sheet, review every frame, and upload footage. Short renders come back in the response; longer ones go to its storage with a signed link. On a laptop or desktop, skip the server: `uf export video.json` writes the file directly.

Full reference: [HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>) and [SELF_HOST.md](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/blob/main/docs/service/SELF_HOST.md>). Limits of the open-source server: one API key, one render at a time with up to 16 waiting, renders stop after 10 minutes, files on local disk.

## Moving an edit over.

The formats differ: a Shotstack Edit is a timeline of tracks and clips; an ultrafast document is a graph of nodes, each with a timing window. Nothing imports either one directly.

### Ask your coding agent

Give it the JSON you send today and ask for the same video as an ultrafast document. With the ultrafast skill installed it knows the format, runs `uf check` until the document is valid, and looks at a contact sheet before it exports.

### Batch renders from data

Merge fields and template variables become a CSV or JSON file of rows: `uf batch` renders one video per row, changing the fields each row names.

```
npx skills add ultrafastmov/ultrafast            # the skill, for your coding agent
uf check video.json && uf sheet video.json --out sheet.png
uf batch video.json --data rows.csv              # one video per row
``` 

## Common questions.

Is there an open-source alternative to Shotstack or JSON2Video?

Yes. ultrafast is an open-source (Apache-2.0 or MIT) engine that renders a JSON document to video on your own GPU, from the command line, over MCP or through a self-hosted HTTP API. Its JSON format is its own, so an existing Shotstack Edit or JSON2Video Movie is rewritten rather than imported; a coding agent with the ultrafast skill can do that.

Can I self-host a JSON-to-video API?

With ultrafast, yes: `docker run --gpus all ghcr.io/ultrafastmov/ultrafast serve` starts an HTTP API and a remote MCP server on one machine with one API key. It renders one job at a time on its GPU. Shotstack, JSON2Video and Creatomate don't offer a self-hosted renderer.

How much does it cost?

The engine is free, including for commercial use; the cost is your own GPU's time. For comparison, Shotstack lists 5¢ to 20¢ per rendered minute by plan, JSON2Video's one credit per second works out to about 17¢ to 42¢ a minute, and Creatomate's pixel-based credits come to about 84¢ a minute of 1080p at 30 fps on its Essential plan billed yearly.

Does ultrafast have a hosted API like Shotstack?

Not yet. Hosted rendering with OAuth connectors for Claude and ChatGPT comes with [ultrafast Cloud](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>), which has a waitlist. Until then you run it yourself, on a Mac with Apple silicon, Linux with a Vulkan GPU, or the Docker image.

Does it work with n8n, Zapier or Make?

There is no ready-made node or app. Any of them can call the HTTP API of `uf serve` with an HTTP request step: POST the document to `/v1/render` with the API key as a bearer token.

## Render one yourself.

Install the engine and export a video on your own GPU.

`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` [Read the quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)

# Changelog · ultrafast release notes

> Every ultrafast release and what it changed, newest first, with the numbers measured. Latest: 0.2.0, smaller files, sooner.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/changelog/

Changelog

# Every release, what changed.

What each ultrafast release changed, newest first, with the numbers measured. The same notes are on [GitHub releases](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/releases>).

  1. **0.2.0** Smaller files, sooner
  2. **0.1.1** Every deliverable from one document
  3. **0.1.0** The first release

0.2.0

23 November 2026Latest

  * [GitHub release](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/releases/tag/v0.2.0>)
  * [Every commit](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/compare/v0.1.1...v0.2.0>)

## Smaller files, sooner

On NVIDIA, exports come out a fifth to a half the size at the same picture, and in about a fifth less time end to end. First runs are quicker, every file says its colours, and the review follows the camera.

[Video: ultrafast 0.2.0: smaller files, sooner](https://ultrafast.mov/media/changelog/ultrafast-0.2.0.mp4)

The benchmark's captioned-footage scene as 300 prints, one per frame, each as thick as its bytes (1 cm = 1 MB). One ultrafast document, rendered by 0.2.0.

### File size at the same picture

  1. Title card: 2.72 MB in 0.1.1, 1.08 MB in 0.2.0.
  2. Chart: 0.73 MB in 0.1.1, 0.35 MB in 0.2.0.
  3. Captioned footage: 9.33 MB in 0.1.1, 2.93 MB in 0.2.0.
  4. Effects reel: 9.04 MB in 0.1.1, 1.59 MB in 0.2.0.

### Export time, end to end

  1. Title card: 0.88 s in 0.1.1, 0.68 s in 0.2.0.
  2. Chart: 0.88 s in 0.1.1, 0.70 s in 0.2.0.
  3. Captioned footage: 1.00 s in 0.1.1, 0.82 s in 0.2.0.
  4. Effects reel: 0.98 s in 0.1.1, 0.76 s in 0.2.0.

The four 10-second scenes of the [benchmark](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/benchmarks>) (300 frames each), exported by 0.1.1 and 0.2.0 on the same RTX 5090 workstation with the same harness, at the standard quality. Times are end to end, from the command to the finished MP4, the median of warm runs.

  * **Files a fifth to a half the size, at the same picture.** On NVIDIA, `--crf` now means libx264's scale (libx265's for HEVC), so `--crf 18` makes the picture libx264 makes at CRF 18. 0.1.1 gave NVENC the number as it was, and its files came out 2 to 4.4 times the size of libx264's. Standard quality also encodes with B-frames and a key frame every 250 frames.
  * **Faster, end to end.** Each frame is encoded in strips across the GPU's encoder engines, the GPU starts with one queue instead of eight, and the encoder's driver starts while the GPU does. The benchmark's scenes export in 0.68 to 0.82 s, against 0.88 to 1.00 s for 0.1.1 on the same machine and harness; one still frame takes 0.20 s, from 0.35 s.
  * **Quicker first runs.** Commands that render and exit compile only the kernels their frames use: a first export after an install or an upgrade takes 1.8 to 2.2 s (2.5 to 2.7 s in 0.1.1).
  * **Colours tagged.** Every YUV export says it is BT.709, limited range, so players don't guess (FFmpeg-based ones guessed BT.601).
  * **`uf review` follows the camera.** Type under a `corner_pin` (a screen or a page in perspective) is measured where the pin puts it, at its size on screen; a label faded out far up a deep stack of layers is no longer reviewed as if it showed. On the SQL notebook example the false "never visible" findings went from 30 to 0.
  * **Fixes.** Two renderers starting at once in one process no longer crash on NVIDIA (the render service's workers could). On macOS, 29.97 fps exports put every frame at its exact time (they were rounded to 1/30 s steps).
  * **Packaging.** The release builds the Claude Desktop extensions and publishes to the MCP Registry from the tag. A `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository runs the MCP server over stdio, so MCP directories such as Glama can build it from the repository, and `plugin.json` and `mcp.json` at the root describe the plugin in the Agent Plugins format GitHub Copilot CLI reads.

The SDKs stay at 0.1.2: nothing in their API changed.

0.1.1

21 November 2026

  * [GitHub release](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/releases/tag/v0.1.1>)
  * [Every commit](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/compare/v0.1.0...v0.1.1>)

## Every deliverable from one document

One document exports to every format a delivery asks for, at any size and frame rate, with one quality setting from draft to master.

  * **Formats and codecs.** H.264, HEVC and AV1 MP4s; ProRes from proxy to 4444 XQ; transparent ProRes 4444 and VP9 WebM (`--alpha`); GIFs; PNG and EXR sequences; and sound alone (WAV, MP3, M4A, FLAC, Opus). The format follows the file name.
  * **Quality levels.** `--quality draft|standard|high|master`: encoder quality, samples and motion blur in one setting. Draft is a fast preview; master is for delivery.
  * **Any size, sharp.** `--size 720p|1080p|4k|WxH` or `--scale`, for `export`, `render` and `frames`. The document is drawn at the new size, not upscaled, so a sharp 4K comes from the same 1080p document.
  * **Any frame rate.** `--fps`.
  * **Estimates as the export will render.** `uf estimate` counts the output size, frame rate and quality level.
  * **The same settings everywhere.** The MCP export tool, the `uf serve` HTTP API and the Python and TypeScript SDKs (0.1.2) take them. The SDKs now default to a local `uf serve`.
  * **Fixes.** Transparent EXR is premultiplied with every ffmpeg; sound-only and GIF outputs are named once; `uf ops | head` exits quietly.
  * **Releases.** crates.io, PyPI, npm, ghcr.io and the Homebrew tap all publish from the tag with trusted publishing.
  * **Claude Desktop and the MCP Registry.** Added to the release on 22 November: a `.mcpb` extension for Claude Desktop on each platform, and the listing `io.github.ultrafastmov/ultrafast` on the official MCP Registry.

```
uf export film.json film.mp4
uf export film.json overlay.mov --codec prores --alpha --size 4k
uf export film.json preview.gif --quality draft --size 480p --fps 15
``` 

0.1.0

21 November 2026

  * [GitHub release](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/releases/tag/v0.1.0>)
  * [Every commit](<https://github.com/ultrafastmov/ultrafast/commits/v0.1.0>)

## The first release

The engine, its JSON document and the tools an agent uses to write, check, review and export video, on macOS and Linux.

  * **The engine.** Every frame is drawn on the GPU, with Metal on macOS and Vulkan on Linux and Windows (WSL2), and no browser in the loop. A video is one JSON document: a format, a graph of nodes, animated params and timing windows.
  * **70 ops.** Type with variable fonts, glyph animators and text on paths; vector paths, SVG and Lottie; images and video; Slang shaders; 3D with image-based light, shadows, depth of field and glass; particles, fluid and feedback simulations; masks, warps, 19 blend modes and looks such as grain, bloom and film looks. Sound is mixed into exports.
  * **The loop.** `uf new` starts from a template, `uf check` finds mistakes without rendering, `uf sheet` draws a contact sheet, `uf review` renders the film and lists text that is unreadable, clipped or on screen too briefly, and flashing, and `uf export` writes the file through the GPU's hardware encoder.
  * **Live.** `uf live` plays a document while an agent edits it over a socket; a parameter edit shows on the next frame.
  * **For agents.** `uf mcp` serves 20 MCP tools. A skill, a Claude Code plugin and a Gemini CLI extension teach the document and the loop.
  * **On your own GPU.** `uf serve` renders over HTTP with one API key, and the Python and TypeScript SDKs (`ultrafastmov` on PyPI and npm) talk to it.
  * **Installs.** Prebuilt archives for macOS on Apple silicon and Linux x86_64, `cargo install ultrafast`, the Homebrew tap and a Docker image on ghcr.io.

## Get the latest.

The install command fetches the newest release, and running it again upgrades. Or `brew upgrade ultrafast`.

`curl -fsSL https://ultrafast.mov/install.sh | sh` [Read the quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)

Want it hosted? [Join the ultrafast Cloud waitlist](<https://ultrafast.mov/cloud/>).


---

# Examples · Films made from JSON documents · ultrafast

> Films made with ultrafast, each with the JSON document that made it: NASA footage cut to its own sound, a podcast clip, data stories, 3D launch films, a simulation and title sequences.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/examples/

Examples

# Every one comes with its document.

12 films, each one JSON document, made by a coding agent. Open any of them to see how it was made.

Real footage

## Cut, captioned, graded.

NASA footage and sound, edited by documents an agent wrote and `review` passed.

[Video: Two launches, one count](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/liftoff.mp4)

### [Two launches, one count](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/liftoff/>)

Apollo 11 and Artemis I lift off in alternating shots, cut to the 1969 launch commentary, with each number in large type and both launches' clocks counting down to zero.

2.39:1 · 1920×804 · 22.5 s · exported in 3.36 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/liftoff.json>)

[Video: Podcast clip](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/podcast.mp4)

### [Podcast clip](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/podcast/>)

A vertical clip of NASA astronaut Mark Vande Hei aboard the space station, cut out of the station on every frame and set over Earth's limb, cloud tops and stars, with four words set huge behind him and captions timed to his voice.

9:16 · 1080×1920 · 27.5 s · exported in 4.07 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/podcast.json>)

Data

## Drawn from the numbers.

Every figure on screen comes from the source credited below.

[Video: Artemis I's route](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/orbit.mp4) 3D rendered by ultrafast

### [Artemis I's route](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/orbit/>)

Artemis I's flown route drawn across lit models of the Earth and Moon, with flight-day and distance counters, and Orion's own view of the Moon at the return flyby.

16:9 · 1920×1080 · 20 s · exported in 7.05 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/orbit.json>)

[Video: The Keeling Curve](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/keeling.mp4)

### [The Keeling Curve](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/keeling/>)

Every monthly mean of carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa since March 1958 draws itself; the camera dives into 2025 to show the seasonal cycle, and the latest month lands large.

4:5 · 1080×1350 · 16 s · exported in 1.50 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/keeling.json>)

[Video: Year in review](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/wrapped.mp4)

### [Year in review](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/wrapped/>)

One script writes a cycling club's year-in-review for each member: distance counts up over the days they rode, their favourite loop draws itself on a contour map, and the climbing rises as mountains.

9:16 · 1080×1920 · 12 s · exported in 1.37 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/wrapped.json>)

[[Video: Year in review: Tomás](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/wrapped-tomas.mp4)Tomás](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/wrapped-tomas.json>)[[Video: Year in review: Oluwaseun](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/wrapped-oluwaseun.mp4)Oluwaseun](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/wrapped-oluwaseun.json>)[[Video: Year in review: Bea](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/wrapped-bea.mp4)Bea](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/wrapped-bea.json>)

[Video: SQL notebook launch](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/ui.mp4)

### [SQL notebook launch](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/ui/>)

A query against NASA's Exoplanet Archive is typed, run, charted and shared in an app that glides and tilts in 3D.

16:9 · 1920×1080 · 16 s · exported in 6.00 s · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/ui.json>)

No footage

## Nothing here was filmed.

The 3D, the simulations and the type are rendered by ultrafast from each document, every frame. Nothing here was filmed or made in another app.

[Video: Pottery class teaser](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/clay.mp4)

3D rendered by ultrafast

### [Pottery class teaser](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/clay/>)

A lump of wet terracotta is centred, opened and pulled into a vase on a turning wheel under window light, beside the class title and its details.

9:16 · 1080×1920 · 10 s · exported in 1.68 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/clay.json>)

[Video: Lens launch](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/product.mp4) 3D rendered by ultrafast

### [Lens launch](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/product/>)

A camera lens that doesn't exist, lit like a studio product shot: light finds the knurled barrel, the focus scale turns, eleven blades stop down and the optics slide apart under callouts.

16:9 · 1920×1080 · 16 s · exported in 4.88 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/product.json>)

[Video: Celadon dish](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/bloom.mp4)

### [Celadon dish](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/bloom/>)

A carving grows across a celadon dish by reaction–diffusion, stepped every frame; the camera closes in on the glaze, then molten glaze floods back over it.

1:1 · 1080×1080 · 15 s · exported in 1.06 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/bloom.json>)

[Video: Concert poster](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/swiss.mp4)

### [Concert poster](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/swiss/>)

A Swiss-style poster for a night of four concerts. Its dial is the score of its own track, and the headline widens and narrows on every beat.

4:5 · 1080×1350 · 12.8 s · exported in 0.72 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/swiss.json>)

[Video: Endless zoom](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/dive.mp4) 3D rendered by ultrafast

### [Endless zoom](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/dive/>)

One camera falls through seven nested worlds (type, vector blades, a chrome torus, ink, shader contours and rings of type) to the wordmark, whose dot holds the first frame again.

16:9 · 1920×1080 · 28 s · exported in 5.65 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/dive.json>)

[Video: Main titles](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/meridian.mp4) 3D rendered by ultrafast

### [Main titles](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/meridian/>)

Main titles for a drama that doesn't exist: a brass compass, a sea chart with a route inking itself across it, star trails over the sea, an armillary sphere, and a lighthouse whose beam lights the title.

2.39:1 · 1920×804 · 24 s · exported in 1.44 s · `review`: 0 findings · [document](<https://ultrafast.mov/examples/meridian.json>)

# Two launches, one count

Apollo 11 and Artemis I lift off in alternating shots, cut to the 1969 launch commentary, with each number in large type and both launches' clocks counting down to zero.

[Video: Two launches, one count](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/liftoff.mp4)

The document

## One JSON file.

This film is one ultrafast document. Read it, diff it, or hand it to your agent as a starting point.

  * [`color_matrix`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-color_matrix>)
  * [`drop_shadow`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-drop_shadow>)
  * [`film_look`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-film_look>)
  * [`gradient`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-gradient>)
  * [`grain`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-grain>)
  * [`over`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-over>)
  * [`shader`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-shader>)
  * [`shape`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-shape>)
  * [`solid`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-solid>)
  * [`text`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-text>)
  * [`transform`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-transform>)
  * [`video`](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/#op-video>)

# Lens launch

A camera lens that doesn't exist, lit like a studio product shot: light finds the knurled barrel, the focus scale turns, eleven blades stop down and the optics slide apart under callouts.

[Video: Lens launch](https://ultrafast.mov/media/examples/product.mp4) 3D rendered by ultrafast

# Op reference · all 70 ops · ultrafast docs

> Every ultrafast op with its ports, params, types and defaults: text, paths, video, captions, blocks, 3D, particles, fluid, shaders, transitions and looks.

URL: https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/

Docs

# 70 ops

Every op with its ports, params, types and defaults. `uf ops` prints the same as JSON.

## Start

  * [Quickstart](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/>)
  * [The document](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/>)

## Guides

  * [Render video from JSON](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/render-video-from-json/>)
  * [Personalized videos from a CSV](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/personalized-videos-from-csv/>)
  * [Make a video with Claude Code](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/claude-code/>)
  * [Lottie to MP4, WebM or ProRes](<https://ultrafast.mov/guides/lottie-to-mp4/>)

## Reference

  * [Ops](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/>)
  * [CLI](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/cli/>)
  * [MCP server](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/mcp/>)
  * [HTTP API](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/api/>)

## For agents

  * [llms.txt](<https://ultrafast.mov/llms.txt>)
  * [This page as Markdown](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/ops/index.md>)

**Groups**

  1. Sources (14)
  2. Compositing (8)
  3. Color (8)
  4. Geometry and warps (8)
  5. 3D (5)
  6. Simulation and particles (4)
  7. Footage, sound and captions (4)
  8. Blocks (1)
  9. Shaders (1)
  10. Looks (17)

Params marked animatable take a constant, `{"keys": [...]}`, `{"expr": "..."}` or a driver (see [params and animation](<https://ultrafast.mov/docs/documents/#params>)). Ports are the node's `inputs`.

## Sources

### solid

flat color

color| color| fill color · default `#000000`  
---|---|---  
  
### gradient

linear, radial or conic gradient

kind| enum(linear | radial | conic)| gradient shape · default `linear`  
---|---|---  
a| color| start color (with b: a two-stop gradient)  
b| color| end color  
stops| text | number[]| "0:#ff0000, 1:#0000ff" or [pos,r,g,b,a,...], up to 8  
space| enum(linear | srgb)| interpolation space; srgb matches CSS/Figma · default `linear`  
start| vec2| linear: start point px · default `[0,0]`  
end| vec2| linear: end point px · default `[0,h]`  
center| vec2| radial/conic center px · default `frame center`  
radius| number| radial radius px · default `max(w,h)/2`  
angle| number| conic start angle, degrees · default `0`  
  
### shape

analytic rectangle / rounded rect / ellipse (SDF, antialiased)

kind| enum(rect | ellipse | circle)| shape · default `rect`  
---|---|---  
color| color| fill (or stroke) color · default `#ffffff`  
center| vec2| center px · default `frame center`  
size| vec2| width and height px · default `[w/4,w/4]`  
radius| number| corner radius px · default `0`  
rotation| number| degrees · default `0`  
scale| number | vec2| scale about the center (size, corners and stroke) · default `1`  
opacity| number| 0..1, fades the shape · default `1`  
stroke| number| outline width px; 0 fills · default `0`  
softness| number| edge softness in output pixels · default `1`  
  
### checker

checkerboard

a| color| first cell · default `#333333`  
---|---|---  
b| color| second cell · default `#666666`  
size| number| cell px · default `32`  
  
### noise

fractal simplex noise between two colors

a| color| low color · default `#000000`  
---|---|---  
b| color| high color · default `#ffffff`  
scale| vec2 | number| px per noise cell · default `[200,200]`  
offset| vec2| pan px · default `[0,0]`  
evolution| number| third noise dimension; animate it · default `0`  
octaves| number| 1..8 · default `4`  
  
### image

still image or image sequence

src| text| file path relative to the document; {frame} / {frame:05} for sequences  
---|---|---  
fit| enum(contain | cover | fill | none)| placement in the frame, or in `rect` (cover there by default); only fill stretches · default `contain`  
rect| vec4| [x,y,w,h] px box the picture goes in, by `fit`; it keeps its aspect ratio  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`  
space| enum(linear | srgb)| interpolation space when scaled; srgb filters the encoded values as browsers do · default `linear`  
fps| number| sequence frame rate · default `document fps`  
first_frame| number| sequence frame number at local time 0 · default `0`  
  
### video

video clip, hardware decoded

src| text| file path  
---|---|---  
fit| enum(contain | cover | fill | none)| placement in the frame, or in `rect` (cover there by default); only fill stretches · default `contain`  
rect| vec4| [x,y,w,h] px box the footage goes in, by `fit`; it keeps its aspect ratio  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`  
space| enum(linear | srgb)| interpolation space when scaled; srgb filters the encoded values as browsers do · default `linear`  
start| number| source seconds at local time 0 · default `0`  
speed| number| playback rate · default `1`  
loop| bool| wrap at the clip's end (else hold the last frame) · default `false`  
time| number| explicit source time (animate for time remapping)  
  
### path

vector path (SVG data or preset), GPU exact-coverage raster

to| text| SVG path data to morph toward; several separated by | to morph through each in turn  
---|---|---  
morph| number| 0 = this path, 1 = `to` (with several targets, 2 = the second, ...); animate it · default `0`  
d| text| SVG path data  
kind| enum(star | polygon | circle | line | polyline | polygon_points)| preset instead of d  
center| vec2| preset center · default `frame center`  
radius| number| preset radius · default `h/4`  
sides| number| star points / polygon sides · default `5 / 6`  
inner_radius| number| star inner radius · default `0.45 r`  
points| number[]| flat [x0,y0,x1,y1,...] for line/polyline/polygon_points  
color| color| paint · default `#ffffff`  
opacity| number| 0..1, fades the whole node (animate for fades) · default `1`  
fill_rule| enum(nonzero | evenodd)| fill rule · default `nonzero`  
trim_start| number| 0..1 of length · default `0`  
trim_end| number| 0..1 of length (animate for draw-on) · default `1`  
stroke| number| stroke width px; 0 fills · default `0`  
join| enum(miter | round | bevel)| stroke joins · default `miter`  
cap| enum(butt | round | square)| stroke caps · default `butt`  
dash| number[]| dash pattern [on, off, ...] px  
dash_offset| number| dash phase px · default `0`  
position| vec2| where the anchor lands, px · default `[0,0]`  
anchor| vec2| pivot in the node's own space, px · default `[0,0]`  
scale| vec2 | number| scale around the anchor · default `[1,1]`  
rotation| number| degrees, clockwise · default `0`  
  
### text

shaped text, GPU exact-coverage raster

text| text| content; \n breaks lines; *word* is emphasis (em_ params), [words]{color=#ffd23f highlight=#ff4d6d} styles a span  
---|---|---  
font| text| family name or font file path · default `Helvetica Neue`  
weight| number| 100..900 · default `400`  
style| enum(normal | italic)| style · default `normal`  
size| number| px · default `64`  
color| color| paint · default `#ffffff`  
opacity| number| 0..1, fades the whole node (animate for fades) · default `1`  
align| enum(left | center | right)| horizontal anchor of each line · default `left`  
valign| enum(top | middle | baseline | bottom)| vertical anchor of the block · default `top`  
width| number| wrap width px  
line_height| number| multiple of size · default `1.2`  
tracking| number| extra px between glyphs · default `0`  
features| text| OpenType features, e.g. "liga=0,ss01"  
variations| text| variable-font axes, e.g. "wdth=80, opsz=144" (weight drives wght; opsz follows size unless set)  
axis_<tag>| number| one variable-font axis, animatable: axis_wdth, axis_SOFT · default `axis default`  
stagger| number| seconds between glyphs for the glyph_* animators · default `0`  
stagger_order| enum(forward | reverse | center | random)| which glyphs go first · default `forward`  
glyph_offset| vec2| per-glyph offset px, keyed in glyph time (t - stagger * order) · default `[0,0]`  
glyph_scale| vec2| per-glyph scale about the glyph's center, glyph time · default `[1,1]`  
glyph_rotation| number| per-glyph rotation degrees, glyph time · default `0`  
glyph_opacity| number| per-glyph opacity, glyph time · default `1`  
reveal| number| glyphs visible (fractional fades) · default `all`  
reveal_softness| number| glyphs the reveal fade spans · default `1`  
reveal_offset| vec2| offset of not-yet-revealed glyphs px · default `[0,0]`  
fill_rule| enum(nonzero | evenodd)| fill rule · default `nonzero`  
skim| bool| glanced at, not read (code, data labels): ultrafast review skips its reading-time check · default `false`  
markup| bool| parse inline styling in text: *emphasis* and [words]{color=#ffd23f weight=800 font="ultrafast:serif" style=italic size=80 highlight=#ff4d6d underline=4 underline_color=#fff rise=10 draw=1} · default `true`  
em_color| color| color of *emphasis* · default `text color`  
em_font| text| face of *emphasis* (e.g. ultrafast:serif for a serif accent) · default `font`  
em_weight| number| weight of *emphasis* · default `weight`  
em_style| enum(normal | italic)| style of *emphasis* (italic is synthesized for faces without one) · default `italic when no em_ param is set`  
em_size| number| size px of *emphasis* · default `size`  
em_highlight| color| marker box behind *emphasis* · default `none`  
em_underline| number| underline thickness px under *emphasis* · default `0`  
em_underline_color| color| underline color · default `em_color`  
em_rise| number| baseline shift px of *emphasis* (up) · default `0`  
em_draw| number| share of the emphasis highlights and underlines drawn, 0..1, one stroke across lines in reading order (animate it) · default `1`  
on_path| text| SVG path data the text follows (closed paths wrap: circular badges); align picks start, middle or end  
path_offset| number| px along the path; animate it to run text along · default `0`  
number| number| show this value instead of text (animate it: counters)  
decimals| number| digits after the point for number · default `0`  
thousands| text| group separator for number ("" for none) · default `,`  
prefix| text| before number, e.g. $  
suffix| text| after number, e.g. % or k  
scramble| number| decoding text: animate 0 (all random) to 1 (the text)  
scramble_chars| text| characters the undecoded ones cycle through · default `A-Z, 0-9, symbols`  
stroke| number| stroke width px; 0 fills · default `0`  
join| enum(miter | round | bevel)| stroke joins · default `miter`  
cap| enum(butt | round | square)| stroke caps · default `butt`  
dash| number[]| dash pattern [on, off, ...] px  
dash_offset| number| dash phase px · default `0`  
position| vec2| where the anchor lands, px · default `[0,0]`  
anchor| vec2| pivot in the node's own space, px · default `[0,0]`  
scale| vec2 | number| scale around the anchor · default `[1,1]`  
rotation| number| degrees, clockwise · default `0`  
  
### svg

an SVG file (logo, icon, illustration) as vector paths: fills, strokes, gradients, text as outlines; `ultrafast import-svg` gives the same as editable nodes

src| text| .svg file (relative to the document)

rotation| number| degrees, clockwise · default `0`  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`  
  
### lottie

a Lottie (Bodymovin) animation as editable ultrafast nodes: shape layers become paths with Lottie's keyframes, transforms stay vector; loops by default

anchor| vec2| pivot px in its fitted space · default `[0,0]`  
scale| vec2 | number| scale · default `[1,1]`  
rotation| number| degrees · default `0`  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`  
  
### code

source code in a panel: syntax-highlighted, optionally typed on with a caret, line numbers, highlighted lines, window chrome

code| text| the source (\n between lines; tabs become 4 spaces)  
---|---|---  
language| enum(rust | python | js | ts | json | bash | go | swift | c | cpp | slang | sql | css | html | text)| how to color it · default `text`  
theme| enum(ultrafast | paper | mono)| colors (paper is light) · default `ultrafast`  
title| text| file name in the title bar  
window| bool| title bar with three dots · default `true`  
background| bool| the panel and its shadow · default `true`  
line_numbers| bool| gutter numbers · default `true`  
highlight| text| lines to mark, e.g. "3" or "2,5-7"  
highlight_at| number| when the marked lines light up · default `0`  
type_speed| number| characters per second typed on (0: all shown) · default `0`  
at| number| when typing starts · default `0`  
caret| bool| a blinking caret while and after typing · default `true`  
font| text| a monospaced face · default `ultrafast:mono`  
size| number| px · default `30 at 1080p`  
line_height| number| multiple of size · default `1.55`  
padding| number| px inside the panel · default `1.4 x size`  
radius| number| panel corner radius px · default `0.55 x size`  
width| number| panel width px · default `fits the longest line`  
position| vec2| top-left of the panel · default `centered`  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`

---|---|---

### stack (in0, in1, in2, in3, in4, in5, in6, in7, in8, in9, in10, in11, in12, in13, in14, in15)

lays its inputs (in0, in1, ...: text, path, shape, svg or stack) out in a column or row by their measured bounds

direction| enum(column | row)| stack downward or rightward · default `column`  
---|---|---  
at| number| seconds at which children are measured (when their entrances have landed) · default `0`  
gap| number| px between children · default `24`  
align| enum(start | center | end)| children across the stack · default `start`  
position| vec2| where the block's anchor goes · default `[0,0]`  
anchor| enum(top_left | top | top_right | left | center | right | bottom_left | bottom | bottom_right)| which point of the block sits at position · default `top_left`  
  
### transition (a, b)

from shot `a` to shot `b` over `duration` s starting `at`: only a renders before, only b after

kind| enum(crossfade | dip | wipe | push | slide | iris | zoom | dissolve | glitch | blur)| how: dip goes through `color`; wipe/push/slide move along `direction`; iris opens from `center`; dissolve burns through noise · default `crossfade`  
---|---|---  
at| number| start, seconds · default `0`  
duration| number| seconds · default `0.8`  
direction| number| degrees: 0 moves rightward, 90 downward · default `0`  
softness| number| edge softness (blur: strength) · default `per kind`  
color| color| dip color; wipe and dissolve edge glow color (dissolve: ember #ff9a4a) · default `#000000`  
glow| number| edge glow strength · default `0 (dissolve 2)`  
center| vec2| iris and zoom center px · default `frame center`  
grain| number| dissolve noise size px · default `160`  
ease| text | number[]| progress easing: a name (in_out_cubic) or [x1, y1, x2, y2] · default `per kind`

### mesh (texture)

---|---|---  
text| text| primitive text: content  
font| text| primitive text: family or file · default `Helvetica Neue`  
weight| number| primitive text: weight · default `400`  
style| enum(normal | italic)| primitive text: style · default `normal`  
size| number| primitive text: size in world units · default `1`  
align| enum(left | center | right)| primitive text: alignment · default `center`  
tracking| number| primitive text: extra spacing (px at 100 px/unit) · default `0`  
line_height| number| primitive text: multiple of size · default `1.2`  
d| text| primitive path: SVG path data  
units| number| primitive path: path px per world unit · default `100`  
depth| number| extrusion depth, world units · default `0.25`  
bevel| number| text/path: 45-degree chamfer on both rims, world units · default `0`  
src| text| .gltf/.glb file instead of a primitive

color| color| base color · default `#cccccc`

ior| number| glass: index of refraction (water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.4) · default `1.45`  
thickness| number| glass: how far refracted rays travel inside, world units (more bends more) · default `0.5`  
dispersion| number| glass: color splitting (try 1..2) · default `0`  
opacity| number| 0..1 · default `1`

### render3d (*)

renders connected meshes/lights/camera (any port names; camera on `camera`)

ambient| number| hemisphere light intensity · default `0.35`  
---|---|---  
sky| color| ambient from above · default `#e6f2ff`
